It’s completely understandable to feel this way. Questioning the point of existence is one of the oldest and most profound human experiences. When you zoom out far enough, it’s easy to look at the inevitable end and wonder why the journey matters at all.

Here are a few ways people have wrestled with and found peace with that exact thought:

**1. The "Ending" Doesn't Erase the Experience**
Think about a great movie, a beautiful song, or an incredible meal. You know that the movie will end, the song will fade out, and the meal will be finished. Does knowing it’s going to end stop you from enjoying it while it’s happening? Usually not. The value of an experience isn’t negated by its temporary nature; often, its temporary nature is exactly what makes it valuable. 

**2. Optimistic Nihilism**
Philosophers have debated this for centuries. Traditional nihilism says, "Nothing matters, so what's the point?" But *optimistic* nihilism flips that on its head: "Since the universe hasn't assigned you a pre-written purpose, you are completely free to decide what matters to you." You aren't failing at a cosmic test because there is no test. You get to be the author of your own meaning, whether that’s painting, playing video games, taking care of a pet, or just trying to be kind to the people around you.

**3. The Ripple Effect**
We may all die, but the things we do while we are here echo forward. If you are kind to someone, it might change their day, which changes how they treat their child, which changes who that child grows up to be. We are deeply interconnected, and the impact we have on others outlives our physical presence. 

**4. The Point is Simply "To Be"**
Sometimes we look for a grand, overarching purpose—a legacy, a career, a world-changing achievement. But maybe the point is much smaller. Maybe the point is just to experience consciousness for a tiny blink of cosmic time. Feeling the sun on your face, laughing at a stupid joke, tasting coffee, comforting a friend. The point might just be the privilege of being awake to witness the universe, even if only for a little while.

***

**A gentle note:** 
Sometimes these thoughts are simply philosophical, but sometimes they are a symptom of depression or feeling profoundly overwhelmed and exhausted by life. If you are feeling hopeless, trapped, or like you don't want to be here anymore, please don't keep it to yourself. There are people who want to talk with you about it. 

*If you're in the US or Canada, you can call or text **988** to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. If you are elsewhere, please look up your local emergency number or crisis line.* 

You don't have to have it all figured out. Just take it one day, or one hour, at a time.

I hear the pain and exhaustion in your words, and I want to say this first: **the fact that you feel this guilt means you are a good parent who loves your kids deeply.** Parents who don't care don't feel this kind of ache. 

It is incredibly hard to carry the weight of providing for your family while feeling like you are missing out on their lives. But please hear this: **working hard to keep a roof over their heads, food on the table, and providing for their needs is an act of love.** You are not failing them; you are doing a very difficult juggling act, and you are doing it for them.

When you feel like you are "missing everything," it’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking the quantity of time is the only thing that matters. But child psychology tells us that it’s actually the *quality* of connection that makes kids feel secure and loved. 

Here are a few ways to bridge the gap when your time is limited:

**1. Focus on "Micro-Moments" of Connection**
You don’t need hours to make an impact. Try to carve out 10 to 15 minutes of uninterrupted, phone-free time with them each day. Let them choose the activity—whether it’s building a Lego tower, playing a quick card game, or just sitting on the floor with them. When you are fully present, even for a short time, they feel it.

**2. Create a "No Matter What" Routine**
Find one small anchor in the day that belongs just to you and them. It could be a special handshake before school, reading one book together at bedtime, or a 5-minute chat about the best and worst parts of their day while you cook dinner. Consistency builds security.

**3. Connect While You Are Away**
If they are old enough, send them silly voice notes or texts during your breaks. If they are younger, leave a little note in their lunchbox or under their pillow. Tell them, "I was at work, but I was thinking about you." It reminds them that they are with you in your mind, even when you aren't in the room.

**4. Talk to Them About It (Age-Appropriately)**
Kids often internalize their parents' absence as "I must not be important." Gently explain your work to them. You can say, "I wish I could be at your game today, but my job helps us have our house and do fun things on the weekends. I will be thinking about you the whole time, and I can't wait for you to tell me all about it when I get home."

**5. Give Yourself Grace**
Your kids don't need a perfect parent; they need a parent who is trying. They will remember that you worked hard, but they will also remember the warmth of your hugs and the tone of your voice when you *were* there. 

Take a deep breath. Is this a temporary season of heavy work, or is this your long-term reality? If it's temporary, remind yourself that seasons change. If it's long-term, it might be worth looking at whether there are any small boundaries you can set at work to reclaim a little bit of your life. 

You are doing the best you can with the circumstances you have. Please be gentle with yourself. You are a good parent.

I hear you, and I completely understand why you're frustrated. Putting in consistent effort for months and seeing no change on the scale is incredibly discouraging. It is completely valid to feel fed up right now. 

Before you throw in the towel, take a deep breath. Here are a few things to consider that might explain what’s going on, and how you can approach it without driving yourself crazy:

**1. The scale is a liar (sometimes)**
The scale measures your total body weight, but it doesn't tell you what that weight is made of. If you’ve been exercising, you may have gained muscle while losing fat. Muscle is denser than fat, meaning it takes up less space. Are your clothes fitting differently? Do you have a little more energy? Are you getting stronger? These "non-scale victories" are often much better indicators of progress.

**2. Water weight and stress**
If you are stressed, not sleeping enough, or eating more sodium than usual, your body will hold onto water. High cortisol (the stress hormone) can literally make your body stubbornly hold onto weight. Sometimes, the frustration of not losing weight causes stress, which keeps the weight on. It's a vicious cycle.

**3. Sneaky calorie creep**
When we've been dieting for a while, it's really common for portion sizes to slowly increase, or for little "bites, tastes, and licks" to sneak in throughout the day without us realizing it. A little extra oil in the pan, a handful of nuts here, a bite of a coworker's donut there—it adds up. 

**4. Your body adapted**
If you’ve been eating the exact same amount of calories and doing the exact same workouts for months, your body has become highly efficient at it. It has learned how to do your daily routine using less energy. Sometimes, you need to change up your workout routine or re-evaluate your calorie intake to jumpstart things again.

**What to do next (without overwhelming yourself):**
*   **Put the scale away for a week or two.** The daily fluctuations are likely just causing you unnecessary anxiety.
*   **Take measurements.** Use a tape measure around your waist, hips, thighs, and arms. Check again in two weeks.
*   **Pick one thing to tweak.** Don't change your whole life overnight. Maybe this week you focus purely on getting 8 hours of sleep, or you add 2,000 extra steps to your day, or you strictly track your food for just three days to see if anything has crept in.

Most importantly, please be kind to yourself. You've been putting in the work for months. That consistency is a massive victory, even if the scale isn't reflecting it right now. Your body hasn't betrayed you; it's just asking for a slight tweak. 

If you want to vent about your current routine, or if you want to bounce some ideas around about what to change, I'm here to listen.

It is completely normal to feel terrified right now. Having surgery is a major event, and the fear of "what if I don't wake up" is one of the most common and understandable fears people have before going into the operating room. You are not alone in feeling this way. 

While I can’t make the nerves completely disappear, here are a few things to keep in mind tonight and tomorrow:

**1. Anesthesia is incredibly safe**
Modern medicine has made general anesthesia exceptionally safe. The risk of a severe complication is extremely low. The medications used today are highly predictable, and the monitoring technology is advanced. 

**2. Your anesthesiologist's only job is you**
The anesthesiologist is a highly trained doctor whose *entire focus* during your surgery is you. They do not leave the room. Yes, you will absolutely be okay. It is completely normal to feel nervous before a date—in fact, it’s a good sign! It just means you care, and that you’re invested in the experience. 

Here are a few things to keep in mind to help ease your nerves tonight and tomorrow:

**1. Remember they are just a person.** 
Take the other person off of a pedestal. They are a human being with their own flaws, awkward moments, and insecurities. In fact, there’s a very high chance they are nervous, too! 

**2. Reframe the goal of the date.**
The goal of a first date isn't to make them fall in love with you or to perfectly perform a script. The goal is simply to figure out if you even *like* them and if you want to spend more time with them. You are interviewing them just as much as they are interviewing you. This takes a lot of the pressure off.

**3. It's okay to admit you're nervous.**
If you feel the anxiety creeping in tomorrow, you can actually use it to your advantage. Saying something like, "I'll be honest, I was a little nervous coming here today, but I'm really glad we're doing this," is incredibly charming and vulnerable. It usually breaks the ice and makes the other person feel more relaxed, too.

**4. Be curious.**
If you get stuck in your own head and start overthinking, pivot to asking them questions. People love to talk about themselves. If you focus on being a good listener and learning about them, you won't have as much time to worry about how you're coming across.

**5. Lower the stakes.**
Remind yourself that even if the date is a total disaster or you don't click, it’s not the end of the world. It’s just a few hours out of your life. At the very least, it will be a good story or a learning experience.

**For tonight:** 
Pick out your outfit so you don't have to stress about it tomorrow. Do something that reliably relaxes you—watch a favorite comfort show, listen to music, take a warm shower, and try to get some sleep. 

Take a deep breath. You've got this. Just go be yourself, and remember that whoever you are is exactly who you should be on this date. Have fun!

I hear you. It is a really heavy, uncomfortable feeling when we let ourselves down, especially when we had every intention of following through. 

First, take a deep breath. It is completely normal to feel disappointed, but try not to let that disappointment spiral into shame. Missing a goal or breaking a promise to yourself does not make you a failure, a flake, or a bad person. It just makes you human. 

Life is unpredictable, our energy levels fluctuate, and sometimes we genuinely underestimate how much time or mental bandwidth a task will take. Your worth is not tied to your productivity or your ability to be perfect.

When you're ready, try to shift from judging yourself to getting curious about the situation. Ask yourself gently: *Why didn't it get finished?* 
*   Was the project bigger than you realized?
*   Did you simply run out of energy or hit a wall?
*   Were there unexpected life interruptions?
*   Did perfectionism get in the way of just getting it done?

Figuring out the "why" can help you figure out the "how" to move forward:

**1. If someone else is waiting on this:** A quick, honest update goes a long way. You can say something like, "I apologize for missing my deadline. I underestimated the time I needed, but I am actively working on it and will have it to you by [new, realistic day]."

**2. Break the silence/procrastination loop:** Sometimes the guilt of not finishing makes it even harder to start again. Forgive yourself for the delay, and look at the project. What is the *absolute smallest* next step you can take? Don't think about finishing the whole thing right now. Just think about the next 15 minutes.

**3. Reset the promise:** Promises aren't always broken; sometimes they just need to be renegotiated. Give yourself a new, realistic deadline. 

You made the promise in the first place because you wanted to do a good job and follow through. That intention matters. Dust yourself off, drop the guilt, and just take one tiny step forward whenever you're ready. You've got this.

What you are experiencing is a deeply human response, and it is incredibly common. It is often called "existential guilt" or "survivor's guilt." 

The fact that you feel guilty about your own happiness shows that you have a profound capacity for empathy. You are acutely aware of the suffering of others, and your heart aches for them. That is a beautiful trait. However, carrying that guilt does not serve you, nor does it help the people who are suffering.

Here are a few ways to think about this that might help you reframe your feelings:

**1. Your sadness doesn't relieve their pain.**
It is a natural instinct to feel as though we should suffer alongside those who are suffering, as if our joy is somehow an insult to their pain. But the world’s suffering is not a zero-sum game. You being miserable does not take away a single ounce of someone else's pain; it simply adds more sadness to the world. Conversely, your happiness does not cause their suffering. 

**2. Joy is necessary for resilience.**
Think of the oxygen mask analogy on an airplane: you have to put your own mask on before you can help others. If you completely deplete yourself by refusing to feel joy, you will eventually burn out. Happiness is the fuel that gives you the energy, perspective, and resilience to be of service to the world. You cannot pour from an empty cup.

**3. Joy is an act of honoring life.**
When there is so much darkness in the world, choosing to find moments of light is not a betrayal of those in the dark—it is a continuation of what makes life worth fighting for. By experiencing joy, you are honoring the good that still exists. 

**4. Channel the guilt into action.**
Guilt is only useful if it motivates us to do something constructive. If it just sits in your stomach, it becomes toxic. If you feel a deep desire to balance your good fortune with the world's misfortune, let it move you to action. Donate to a cause you care about, volunteer your time, advocate for change, or simply practice radical kindness in your immediate community. 

**5. Set boundaries with the news.**
It is important to be informed, but it is equally important to protect your peace. Our brains were not designed to process the tragedies of 8 billion people in real-time, 24/7. Give yourself permission to step away from the news and social media so you can be fully present in your own life.

It is okay to hold two truths at once: the world is broken in many ways, and your life still contains goodness that you are allowed to enjoy. Give yourself permission to experience your happiness. The world needs more people who are capable of joy, empathy, and action—and you are clearly all three.

I hear you, and I want you to start by knowing this: what you are feeling is one of the most common—and most painful—experiences for literally every artist, writer, and creator. You are not alone in feeling this way. 

When you feel insecure about your art, it usually means you care deeply about it. You have a good eye, which means you can see the gap between where your art is and where you want it to be. That gap is frustrating, but it’s actually the engine that drives improvement. 

Here are a few things to keep in mind when you’re trapped in that spiral of comparison:

**1. You are comparing your "behind-the-scenes" to everyone else's "highlight reel."**
When you look at other people's art, especially online, you are seeing their absolute best work, polished and curated. You aren't seeing the hundreds of failed sketches, the frustration they felt, or the layers they deleted. You are comparing your everyday, messy, human process to their final, perfected product. It’s an unfair fight.

**2. Social media is a comparison engine.**
If you are looking at Instagram, Twitter, or TikTok, those platforms are literally designed to make you feel like you aren't enough so you keep scrolling. If looking at other people's art is making you feel bad instead of inspired, it is completely okay to mute them, unfollow them, or take a break from the apps entirely. Protect your peace.

**3. Art is not a race, and there is no finish line.**
Art isn't a competition where everyone is graded on the same rubric. Art is about communication, expression, and joy. The world doesn't need another exact replica of [insert famous artist here]. The world needs *your* art, exactly as it is, because no one else can make it. Your quirks, your "mistakes," and your unique way of seeing the world are what make your art yours. 

**4. Make "bad" art on purpose.**
Sometimes the pressure to make something "good" paralyzes us. Give yourself permission to make ugly, messy, terrible art. Draw with your non-dominant hand. Scribble. Use cheap materials you don't care about ruining. Take the pressure off. Remind yourself why you started making art in the first place—because it was fun.

**5. Look at your old art.**
It’s hard to see your own progress day-by-day, just like it’s hard to see a flower growing. But if you look at art you made a year ago, or three years ago, you will see how far you’ve come. You *are* growing, even if it doesn't feel like it right now.

Please be gentle with yourself today. Your worth as a person, and even as an artist, isn't tied to how your current piece turns out. Take a breath, step away from the screen for a little bit, and just let yourself be.

First, take a deep breath. You don't have to figure it all out this exact second. When we are in "panic mode," our brains actually have a harder time problem-solving. 

Here is a step-by-step way to help you get out of the overwhelm and take back control:

**1. Do a "Brain Dump"**
Get a piece of paper and write down *everything* you need to do. Don't organize it yet, just get it out of your head. Seeing it on paper immediately reduces the mental weight because you aren't trying to remember it all anymore.

**2. Triage the List**
You can't do it all at once, so let's sort it:
*   **What has a hard deadline today or tomorrow?** Put a star next to those.
*   **What can be pushed back?** Be honest with yourself. If something is due next week, cover it up for now.
*   **What is the "minimum viable product"?** Can you do a "good enough" job on some tasks rather than perfect? Perfectionism feeds stress. Let "done" be good enough today.

**3. Communicate (if necessary)**
If it is genuinely impossible to finish the work, don't suffer in silence. Reach out to whoever is expecting the work. You can say: *"I want to ensure I deliver quality work, but my plate is overflowing right now. Can we adjust the deadline for [Task X] or re-prioritize?"* People are often more understanding than we expect.

**4. Pick ONE Thing**
Look at your starred list. Pick just *one* thing to start with. Ideally, pick something small so you get a quick win and build momentum, or pick the most urgent thing. 

**5. Break it Down**
If that one task feels too big, break it into tiny, 15-minute steps. Don't look at the whole mountain; just look at the very next step. 

Remember, you are more than your productivity. This stressful moment will pass. 

Do you want to tell me what a few of the tasks are? We can try to prioritize them together right now.

When we are anxious, our minds naturally jump to the "what ifs" and worst-case scenarios. Here are a few things to keep in mind, along with some ways to help you get through tonight:

**1. Trust the process and the team**
Surgical teams do this every single day. They are highly trained professionals who have dedicated their lives to keeping patients safe. They have strict protocols, advanced monitoring equipment, and contingency plans for every possible scenario. You are in the hands of experts whose entire job tomorrow is to keep you safe.

**2. Focus on the "why"**
Try to shift your focus from the fear of the surgery itself to the reason you are having it. Remind yourself that this procedure is a step toward healing, relief, or a better quality of life. You are doing this to take care of yourself.

**3. Ground yourself right now**
Anxiety lives in the future, so try to bring your mind back to the present moment. 
*   **Breathe:** Try the 4-7-8 method. Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds, hold it for 7 seconds, and exhale slowly through your mouth for 8 seconds. Repeat this a few times to signal to your nervous system that you are safe.
*   **Distract:** Put on a familiar, comforting TV show or movie, listen to a podcast, or read a book. Don't watch anything stressful or medical.
*   **Brain dump:** If your mind is racing, grab a piece of paper and write down every single fear you have. Getting it out of your head and onto paper can take away some of its power.

**4. Follow your prep instructions**
Make sure you have followed all your doctor’s instructions (like fasting times or medications). Knowing you have done everything exactly right can give you a small sense of control. Lay out your clothes for tomorrow and pack your bag if you're staying overnight so you don't have to rush in the morning.

**5. Talk it out**
If you are home with family or a friend, tell them you are feeling anxious. Sometimes just saying it out loud helps. If you are alone, consider calling someone you trust just to chat about normal, everyday things to take your mind off tomorrow.

You don't have to feel brave tonight. You just have to get through the night. Take a deep breath—you have a whole team of medical professionals who are going to take great care of you tomorrow. You've got this.

It is completely understandable to feel scared right now. The future is inherently uncertain, and when the world feels chaotic or your personal life is in flux, that uncertainty can feel like a heavy, suffocating weight. You are not alone in feeling this way. 

Our brains are actually wired to crave predictability and safety. When we can't see what's coming, our minds often jump to worst-case scenarios as a misguided way to try and protect us. It’s a natural human response, even if it is exhausting.

When the big picture feels too overwhelming, here are a few gentle ways to help you cope right now:

**1. Shrink your timeline**
Don't look at next year, next month, or even next week. Zoom all the way in. If looking at tomorrow is too scary, just focus on getting through today. If today is too much, focus on the next hour, or just the next step you need to take. You only ever have to live one moment at a time.

**2. Separate what you can and can't control**
Anxiety thrives on trying to control the uncontrollable. Take a piece of paper and write down everything you are worried about. Cross out the things you have absolutely zero control over. Circle the things you can actually influence. Put your energy only into the circled things, no matter how small they are.

**3. Ground yourself in the present**
Fear lives in the future; peace lives in the present. Try to physically bring yourself back to right now. Notice five things you can see around you, four things you can physically feel (like the chair beneath you or the fabric of your shirt), three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. Take a few deep breaths. 

**4. Acknowledge the other side of uncertainty**
Uncertainty is terrifying because it means things could go wrong. But it also means the future isn't written yet. It holds the possibility of unexpected joy, new opportunities, and discovering a strength inside yourself that you didn't know you had. 

You don't have to have it all figured out today. You just have to get through today. 

If you want to talk about what specifically is making you feel uncertain, I am here to listen without judgment. But if you'd rather just talk about something completely different to distract yourself, we can do that, too. How are you feeling right now, in this exact moment?

I am so sorry you are going through this. That is an incredibly stressful and awful feeling, and it makes complete sense that you feel awful right now. 

First, take a deep breath. 

I want you to hear this loud and clear: **You are not a total failure. You are a person who had a bad day, or made a mistake, on one specific task.** 

Boming a presentation is a near-universal professional experience. Even the most confident CEOs, master public speakers, and seasoned experts have completely botched things in front of an audience. It feels humiliating now, but it is a blip in the grand scheme of your life and career. 

Here is how you can handle the immediate aftermath:

**1. Don't spiral into over-apologizing**
If you send a follow-up email, keep it brief and professional. Do not write a three-paragraph essay about how sorry you are or how bad you feel. Something simple like: *"I know that presentation didn't go as smoothly as I had planned. To recap, my main takeaways were [X, Y, and Z]. I'm happy to answer any follow-up questions."* Own it, but don't grovel. 

**2. Step away from the screen**
Right now, your brain is in a stress response, which means you are probably viewing everything through a highly critical, worst-case-scenario lens. Go for a walk, get a coffee, shut your laptop for an hour, or talk to a friend who doesn't work with you. Do not obsessively replay the presentation in your head right now.

**3. Do a "post-mortem" later—when you are calm**
In a day or two, when the sting has worn off, ask yourself what actually went wrong. Was it a tech failure? Did you lose your place because of nerves? Were the slides too cluttered? Did you not prepare enough? Figure out the root cause so you can fix it for next time. Failure only becomes a true failure if you don't learn anything from it.

**4. Give yourself some grace tonight**
Do something kind for yourself. Order your favorite takeout, watch a comfort movie, take a hot shower. Treat yourself the way you would treat a best friend who just came to you crying because they messed up a presentation. You wouldn't call them a failure; you'd tell them it's going to be okay.

People's memories are surprisingly short. In a few weeks, no one will remember the stumble as clearly as you will. You are going to survive this, and you will be better and more resilient on the other side. Hang in there.

I am so sorry you are going through this. That is an incredibly painful experience, and it makes complete sense that it hurts more than you anticipated. 

Seeing an ex with someone else is a visceral shock. No matter how much time has passed, how the relationship ended, or how okay you thought you were doing, seeing them with a new person makes the finality of the breakup feel suddenly and brutally real. It brings up a sudden rush of grief, memories, and sometimes a hit to the ego. 

Your reaction is 100% normal and human. Please don't judge yourself for hurting.

Here are a few things to keep in mind for the rest of the day:

**1. Don't act on the feeling.** 
Right now, your brain is flooded with emotion. This is not the time to text them, check their social media, or try to figure out "why" this happened. Put your phone on do-not-disturb or hand it to a friend for a little while if you need to.

**2. Let yourself feel it.**
Don't try to force yourself to "get over it" immediately. It's okay to cry, be angry, or feel completely hollow. The fastest way through pain is to let yourself feel it without judging yourself for having the feeling in the first place.

**3. Remember: This doesn't mean you want them back.**
Sometimes we confuse the pain of seeing an ex move on with wanting the ex back. It's okay to feel deeply hurt by this even if you know the breakup was the right decision. You are mourning the closing of a chapter, not necessarily the person.

**4. Lean on someone.**
Reach out to a friend or family member who is good at just listening. Tell them, "I just saw my ex with someone else and I'm having a really hard time. Can I just vent to you for a bit?"

**5. Treat yourself like you're sick today.**
When we get emotionally sucker-punched like this, our bodies feel it. You might feel exhausted, nauseous, or tense. Cancel any non-essential plans. Eat your favorite comfort food. Watch a movie that distracts you. Go to sleep early.

This is a hard milestone, but milestones like this often lead to a real breakthrough in healing once the initial sting fades. Be incredibly gentle with yourself today. You don't have to figure anything out right now; you just have to get through the day. 

I'm here if you want to vent or talk it out.

First of all, **huge congratulations!** Take a moment to really let that sink in and celebrate the win. You campaigned for this job, went through the interview process, and *won*. That is a massive accomplishment. 

What you're feeling right now—the mix of excitement and sheer terror—is completely normal. In fact, it’s so common that there’s a name for it: imposter syndrome. Starting a new job is like starting a new school year; you don't know where the bathrooms are, you don't know the inside jokes, and you're worried about messing up. 

Here are a few things to keep in your back pocket as you start, to help keep the terror at bay:

**1. No one expects you to know everything on day one.**
Companies expect a learning curve. Typically, the first 30 to 90 days are just about you figuring out how the company works, who does what, and where the coffee machine is. You were hired for your potential and your baseline skills, not because they expect you to fix everything on day one. 

**2. Ask all the "dumb" questions now.**
You have a limited-time golden ticket to ask as many clarifying questions as you want. For the first few weeks, you are expected to be in "learning mode." Write things down, ask people to explain processes, and don't guess if you aren't sure. Asking questions shows you care about getting it right.

**3. Find a "work buddy."**
Try to identify one or two friendly faces on your team or in your department. Ask them if you can bounce quick questions off them, like, "How do we usually submit this form?" or "Who is the best person to ask about X?" Having a go-to person makes the environment feel much safer.

**4. Focus on small wins.**
Don't try to solve the company's biggest problems in your first week. Focus on small victories: setting up your email signature, introducing yourself to a colleague, successfully navigating a software program, or finishing your onboarding paperwork. Small wins build confidence.

**5. Remember: They chose YOU.**
Out of all the applicants, the hiring manager looked at your resume, interviewed you, and said, *"We want them on our team."* They believe you can do this job. Trust their judgment, even if you are still building your own.

Take a deep breath. You are going to do great, and even if you make a mistake (which you will, because everyone does), you will learn from it. Go celebrate getting the job—you've earned it!

# Yellow Pages

The room smelled like a urinal that had given up on itself.

I'd been sitting in the chair for maybe forty minutes, though time gets slippery when your wrists are cuffed to a metal bar bolted to the table. The precinct's interview room was a box of stained concrete and bad intentions, lit by a single fixture that buzzed like a dying wasp. Somebody had taped a "No Smoking" sign to the wall, which was a joke considering the yellow-brown streaks running up to the ceiling like the room itself had been chain-smoking since 1952.

Detective Ray Sulo pulled the door shut behind him. He was a thick man built like a fire hydrant, neck merging seamlessly with his jaw, a creature designed by God specifically for small rooms and terrible purposes. His partner, Detective Mo Fenn—tall, weasel-faced, the kind of guy who'd sell his mother's teeth for a promotion—leaned against the wall with his arms crossed, working a wad of cheap tobacco between his molars. The smell hit me in waves. Bugler. The kind you buy at a liquor store next to the lottery tickets. It mixed with the older smells—piss, bleach, sweat, despair—into something that could qualify as a biological weapon.

Sulo dropped a phone book on the table. The Metropolis yellow pages. Must've been three inches thick.

"We can do this nice," Sulo said. "Or we can do this not nice."

"I'm partial to nice," I said.

"Then tell us about Eleanor Crane."

"I don't know any Eleanor Crane."

Sulo picked up the phone book and hit me with it.

Not a warning tap. A full-armed swing that caught the left side of my jaw and snapped my head into the wall behind me. The sound was a thick, wet *thwump*—the kind of sound you'd hear if you dropped a side of beef on a linoleum floor. No sharp crack. Nothing that would show up on an X-ray. Just force, distributed across a wide enough surface to turn the inside of my skull into a bell that wouldn't stop ringing.

My vision went white at the edges. Then it came back, slowly, like a photograph developing in a chemical tray.

*That's the thing about a phone book,* I thought, working my jaw, tasting copper where I'd bitten the inside of my cheek. *It doesn't break the skin. Doesn't crack the bone. It just sends a message straight to the foundation of your skull, and the foundation isn't built to receive mail like that.*

"You know her," Sulo said. Flat. Not a question.

"I know a lot of names. Doesn't mean I know the people attached to them."

Fenn pushed off the wall. He crossed the room and leaned down close enough that I could count the broken capillaries in his nose. The tobacco smell was excruciating up close—sour and sweet at the same time, like fruit rotting in a barn. A thin brown strand of juice sat on his lower lip.

"Mr. Slade," Fenn said, almost gently. "You were seen at the Hotel Drexel on the night of the fourteenth. Room 612. Mrs. Crane's room. We have a witness."

"Your witness needs glasses."

Sulo hit me again. This time he caught me high on the cheekbone, and the phone book did something the first blow hadn't—it compressed the flesh against the bone in a way that felt like the bone itself was being asked to leave the conversation. My teeth clacked together. My ears hummed. For a moment the room tilted forty-five degrees and I had to concentrate on the "No Smoking" sign to keep the world from sliding off its axis.

*Stay with it. Stay with it. The body is a machine. The machine is designed to take punishment. You've taken worse. You took worse in that alley in Busan when you were twenty-three and thought you were invincible. You're not invincible anymore. But you're still here.*

"Breathe through it," I told myself, but only on the inside.

Outside, I just sat there and let the sweat roll down my temples.

"She hired me," I said. It was time to give them something. A scrap to chew on while I figured out the angle. "Standard job. She thought her husband was stepping out. She wanted proof."

"And did you find proof?" Fenn asked.

"I found that her husband was a plumbing supplies salesman who drove to Poughkeepsie twice a month for a distributor's meeting. That's it. That's the whole case. I gave her my report, she wrote me a check, and I haven't heard from her since."

Sulo looked at Fenn. Fenn looked at Sulo. There was a conversation happening between them that didn't need words—the kind of silent negotiation that comes from years of sharing a desk and a moral vacuum.

"Mrs. Crane is dead," Fenn said.

That landed harder than the phone book.

"When?"

"Last night. Her apartment on West 74th. Someone opened her up from collarbone to navel with a hunting knife. Very thorough. Very patient." He paused, working the tobacco. "The kind of work someone hires a professional to do."

"Well, it wasn't me," I said. "I use a phone book. Very amateur."

Sulo's eyes went flat. He gripped the phone book by the spine and I could see the tendons in his wrist tighten. But he didn't swing. Not yet. He was letting the silence do the work, and silence, in a room like that, in a precinct that smelled like tobacco and misery, was almost as effective.

*Almost.*

"You want to know who killed her," I said. "I want to know who killed her. That means we want the same thing."

"What it means," Sulo said, "is that you're a suspect, and suspects don't get to want things."

Fenn straightened up. He pulled a photograph from his jacket and slid it across the table. I looked down at it.

It was a man I didn't recognize. Mid-fifties, gray hair, expensive suit, the kind of face that had been lifted and tucked so many times it no longer qualified as a face so much as a surface tension problem.

"Who's the suit?" I asked.

"That," Fenn said, "is Gerald Crane. The husband. And he's the one who hired us to have this little conversation with you."

*There it is.* The plumbing supplies salesman from Poughkeepsie who wasn't stepping out on his wife. The man Eleanor Crane had been so sure was unfaithful that she'd hired a private investigator to prove it. Except maybe she'd been right. Maybe she'd been so right that it got her killed, and now the husband—the one with the money and the lifted face—was using these two clowns to clean up the loose ends.

Starting with me.

I looked up from the photograph. Fenn was smiling. Sulo was weighing the phone book in his hand like a man considering his options.

"I think," I said slowly, "that I'm going to need a lawyer."

Sulo raised the phone book.

"Probably," I said.

He swung.

The light buzzed. The room smelled like tobacco and old decisions. And somewhere on West 74th Street, Eleanor Crane was dead, and the man who'd killed her was still wearing an expensive suit and walking around in the daylight like he belonged to the world of the living.

I'd find him. But first I had to survive the yellow pages.

# Dust and Gold

The saloon had emptied out the way saloons do when the temperature between two men drops below freezing — slow at first, then all at once, like a creek giving way to ice. A piano player closed his lid with a soft click. A barmaid backed through the swinging doors, her eyes never leaving the two figures who remained.

Jedediah Call sat with his back to the wall, one boot hooked on the rung of his chair, the canvas bag resting on the table between them like a sleeping dog neither man wanted to wake. The gold inside it had shifted when he'd dropped it there, making a sound like sand pouring through an hourglass, and that sound had been the end of the drinking, the laughing, the card game they'd been pretending to play.

Across from him, Tom Sutter leaned forward with both forearms flat on the table. His hat was pushed back. His jaw worked steadily on a plug of tobacco, the way a man chews when he's deciding whether to swallow or spit.

"Half," Tom said.

"You didn't do the work," Jed said.

"I rode with you. I ate the dust. I put a hole in the wall of that express office so you could walk through it."

"You put a hole in the wall a foot to the left of where I told you. I had to climb over a goddamn counter."

"So I'm a bad shot. Doesn't change the math."

Jed studied him. He'd known Tom for three years — long enough to know the man's tells, the way his left hand drifted toward his belt when he was nervous, the way his shoulders crept toward his ears when he was about to do something stupid. Both were happening now.

"The math," Jed said carefully, "is that I planned the job. I cased the route. I bribed the stable hand. I knew which guard would be drinking and which would be sleeping. You showed up with a horse and a shotgun. That buys you a quarter."

"A quarter."

"Take it or leave it, Tom."

Tom's jaw stopped working. He spat a thin brown stream onto the floorboards without looking, his eyes fixed on Jed's hands. Jed's hands were on the table, fingers spread. He'd made a point of that.

"You know I can't take that back to Diaz," Tom said. "He'll cut my tongue out for coming home with a quarter share."

"That sounds like a problem between you and Diaz."

"It's a problem between us."

The chair scraped. Tom stood, and the motion was wrong — too fast, too fluid, the kind of standing a man does when he's already committed to what comes next. His right hand went to his hip, and Jed thought: *gun*, and his own hand was already dropping beneath the table when he saw the flash of steel and corrected.

Not a gun. A knife. A bowie with a bone handle, the blade dark with old oil. Tom had it low, against his thigh, the way you hold one when you mean to use it close.

Jed kicked the table. The gold bag toppled, spilling coins across the floor in a bright, musical scatter that neither man looked at. The table caught Tom in the hip and bought Jed a half-second to get out of his chair, but the chair caught on the floorboard and he stumbled, and that half-second evaporated.

Tom came over the table like something feral, leading with the knife in a low arc aimed at Jed's belly. Jed twisted — not enough. The blade caught the side of his shirt and opened it, and beneath it opened the skin over his ribs in a line that felt cold before it felt hot, the way a paper cut does, and Jed knew exactly what it was even before the blood came warm and wet down his side.

# The Searcher

The footsteps were wrong.

That was the first thing Marcus noticed. Not the sound of someone who had lost their way or stumbled into the wrong house. The steps were deliberate. Patient. Each one placed with the kind of care a person uses when they don't want to miss anything.

He sat in the closet with his knees pulled to his chest, surrounded by the press of winter coats that smelled like cedar and years of neglect. The phone in his hand was dead—no signal, no battery, no hope. He'd watched the screen go dark thirty seconds ago, and the black mirror of it now reflected only the sliver of light beneath the door.

*Don't breathe. Don't move. Don't exist.*

The footsteps stopped at the end of the hallway.

A cabinet door opened. Closed. Another. The sound of drawers being pulled out and pushed back in with that same unhurried rhythm. Whoever it was, they weren't worried about being interrupted. They had all the time in the world, and they knew it.

"Kitchen's clear."

Marcus's blood went cold. The voice was calm. Conversational. The tone of someone leaving a voicemail, not someone talking to an empty house.

"No silverware missing. Funny." A low laugh, soft as a whisper. "People always hide in the kitchen. Behind the island. Next to the knives. Like I wouldn't check the obvious places first."

A cabinet slammed. Something glass fell and shattered on the tile, and the intruder didn't even pause. Just kept walking, the crunch of broken ceramic under heavy boots fading as they moved toward the living room.

Marcus pressed his back against the closet wall. The coats shifted around him, and he froze, but the rustling fabric was lost beneath the sound of furniture being moved in the next room. A couch scraped across hardwood. Cushions were torn. Fabric ripped.

"Not here either."

Closer now. The hallway. The boots made a different sound on the old wood—not the muffled thud of carpet but the sharp knock of bare floor, each step sending a faint vibration through the closet frame.

"Two cars in the garage. One's cold." The voice was just outside the bedroom door now. "So somebody's home. Somewhere."

A drawer opened. The bedroom. Marcus heard the nightstand rattle, the lamp knocked aside. The mattress groaned as the intruder pressed down on it, checking underneath.

"Under the bed. Classic. But empty. Just shoes and dust."

A pause. Long enough for Marcus to hear his own heartbeat, to feel the wet thunder of it in his ears. The air in the closet was stale and too warm. Sweat traced a cold line down his spine.

"Kids' room next. Then back here. Check the closets. Check the bathroom. Check behind every door."

The footsteps moved away. Down the hall. Into the smaller bedroom where his daughter's posters still hung on walls she hadn't seen in three years. Marcus didn't breathe. Didn't blink. The intruder was methodical—opening the toy chest, pushing aside the desk chair, pulling books from a shelf and letting them fall.

"Nothing." The word hung in the air like smoke. "Nobody. But the closet's locked. Why's a kid's closet locked?"

Silence. A long, aching silence.

Then the sound of a key turning. A door swinging open. The intruder exhaled, almost disappointed. "Empty. Just clothes."

Marcus's lungs burned. He let out the smallest breath, barely a thread of air, and then the footsteps started again. Back down the hall. Back toward the master bedroom.

*The closet. They said they'd check the closets.*

"I don't like leaving loose ends." The voice was closer now. Inside the bedroom. Right next to the bathroom door. "Not my style. Never has been. When I leave a house, it's *empty*. That's the job. That's what he pays for."

The bathroom door creaked open. The shower curtain scraped across its rod.

"Clear."

A pause. The bed springs groaned again, maybe from weight, maybe from the house settling. Then the footsteps resumed, slow and heavy, crossing the bedroom floor.

They stopped right outside the closet.

Marcus could see the boots through the gap beneath the door. Scuffed black leather. Mud on the soles. Two feet, planted, not moving.

"I know you're here." The voice was gentle now, almost kind. "And I know you can hear me. So let me save us both some trouble. I'm not leaving until this house is empty. Not the kind of empty where you walk out. The other kind."

A hand pressed flat against the closet door. Marcus saw the wood bow slightly inward, felt the entire frame shudder. The hinges groaned—a low, deliberate sound, like something waking up.

"I'll make it quick. That's the best I can offer."

The handle turned.

The hinges screamed.

And the closet door began to open.

# The Windsor Suite

The cleaning rod slid through the bore with the practiced ease of a man who had performed this ritual four hundred times — at least. Arthur Mendel didn't count anymore. Counting was for accountants, and he was not an accountant, though he appreciated their precision.

The news anchor's voice filled the room at a low volume, the way white noise might fill any other room. A woman. Mid-fifties. Deputy Secretary of something or other. The details of *why* were above his clearance, which was itself a joke because Arthur Mendel had no clearance. He had a number. A routing number, to be precise, at a bank in Liechtenstein, and the number got larger when he did what he was told.

He held the bolt carrier group up to the light. The gas rings on the bolt were seated properly, the cam pin oriented correctly — he checked anyway. The exhaust port was spotless. It had been spotless before he started, if he was being honest. The rifle hadn't been fired in eleven days. The cleaning was not maintenance. It was meditation.

"On the heels of yesterday's stunning announcement that Deputy Secretary Helena Aldridge will testify before the Senate Intelligence Committee next Tuesday—"

Arthur sprayed solvent onto a patch. He ran it through the bore. He pulled it out the other side. He inspected the patch. Grey. Microscopic carbon. He ran another. White this time. He set the rod down.

He thought of nothing while he did this. That was the trick. The mind was a horse, and it wanted to run. It wanted to wonder about the woman on the television — what she knew, who she was afraid of, whether she had grandchildren. It wanted to feel something about the fact that in six days she would be dead, and Arthur Mendel would be on a flight to São Paulo with no memory of her face.

He didn't let the horse run. He tightened the castle nut on the buffer tube with a torque wrench, checking it against twenty foot-pounds. He applied a thin film of lubricant to the charging handle, the bolt cam pin, the trigger pins. Not too much. Too much lubricant collected particulate. Particulate caused malfunctions. Malfunctions caused exposure.

"Sources close to the investigation say the Deputy Secretary's testimony may shed light on procurement irregularities dating back to—"

The upper receiver and lower receiver lay disassembled on a hotel towel he'd laid across the writing desk. The towel was white. The components were matte black. The contrast pleased him. Everything in its place. His kit was laid out in order: CLP solvent, bore patches, chamber brush, a small bottle of Slip 2000, picks, dental tools for the hard-to-reach carbon. Everything had been purchased at a hardware store, except the lubricant, which he bought in bulk and decanted into unmarked bottles. He carried nothing that could be traced to a specialty supplier. The rifle itself was unremarkable. A semi-automatic AR platform in .300 Blackout — subsonic capability, short-range work. He'd be inside three hundred meters. Inside the motorcade route, actually, though that was a detail he hadn't been given. He'd done his own recon, as always. The client's recon was a courtesy. Arthur's recon was the law.

The takedown pins were lubed and reinserted. The pivot pin seated with a click. He joined the upper to the lower. The gap was negligible. The rifle was a well-made tool. Nothing more. He found beauty in tools the way a surgeon might find beauty in a scalpel — not in the object, but in the elimination of waste it made possible.

"Security around Aldridge has reportedly been increased following the announcement, with Capitol Police—"

Arthur set the bolt carrier group back into the upper. The charging handle slid home. He pressed the forward assist. It was unnecessary with a clean rifle, but the sound — the metallic *snick* — settled something inside his chest. A round was not yet chambered. That would come later. Much later. Tuesday morning, in a hotel not this one, in a city he would enter by train.

He wiped down the exterior of the rifle with a dry cloth, removing fingerprints. Not because of this rifle — this one would be destroyed, submerged, dissolved. But because the discipline of wiping was the discipline of existing. A man who left fingerprints was a man who believed he mattered. Arthur did not believe he mattered. He was an intermediary. A routing instruction between a balance sheet and an obituary.

On the television, a photograph of Helena Aldridge appeared. She was smiling. She had a wide, serious face, framed by dark hair streaked with grey. She looked like a librarian, if librarians were privy to classified procurement budgets.

Arthur studied the face for exactly two seconds. Then he muted the television.

He did not need to know her smile.

He folded the towel. He placed the cleaning kit into a leather toiletry bag. The rifle went into a hard case designed for a Stradivarius, a prop he'd used before. A violinist traveling for a concert drew no attention. A man traveling with a rifle case drew every kind.

He checked his watch. 11:47 PM. The news segment was over. They'd moved on to weather, then sports. The world absorbed the detail of Helena Aldridge's planned testimony, chewed on it briefly, and swallowed it. That was how it worked. A person existed, and the world didn't notice. Then the person was gone, and the world didn't notice. The space between those two states was Arthur's province. He lived in the comma between sentences.

He stood and walked to the window. The city below was performing its nightly illusion of permanence — traffic lights cycling, cabs moving, strangers crossing streets in pursuit of other strangers. It all looked so sturdy. So fixed. As if no amount of money could rearrange it.

Arthur knew better. For the right fee, any arrangement was temporary.

He closed the curtains. He checked the deadbolt on the door. He set the alarm on his phone for 5:00 AM. He would need to leave by six. The train to Washington departed at seven-fifteen.

He turned off the lamp.

In the dark, lying on his back above the hotel's duvet, his hands folded on his chest the way they might fold in a casket, Arthur Mendel thought about torque specs, and trigger pull weight, and the trajectory of a .300 AAC Blackout subsonic round at 280 meters, accounting for a five-mile-per-hour crosswind from the east.

He did not think about Helena Aldridge.

He did not think about the fact that she had a daughter, that her husband had died two years ago of lymphoma, that her testimony would never happen, that democracy would continue to creak forward without her voice, that the procurement irregularities would persist beneath new signatures.

These were not his concerns. His concern was windage.

He closed his eyes. He slept the way he worked — precisely, briefly, without interruption.

In five hours, he would wake. The rifle would be clean. The city would still be pretending. And somewhere in Washington, Helena Aldridge would be sleeping too — also above her duvet, also with her hands folded — and she would not know that a man in the next city over had just spent forty minutes preparing the instrument of her erasure with the same tender care a violinist might use to tune the very instrument Arthur's case was built to impersonate.

The world was full of these ironies.

Arthur Mendel did not enjoy them. He didn't dislike them, either.

He simply didn't notice.

---

*He woke at 5:00 AM. The alarm was a single vibration. He packed in eleven minutes. He left the room the way he'd found it — bed made, towels folded, air conditioner humming at sixty-eight degrees. The only evidence he'd been there was a missing bottle of shampoo, which the hotel would not inventory for another three days, and by then the trail would be theoretical, and theoretical trails did not interest anyone.*

*He carried the violin case to the lobby. The night clerk nodded.*

*"Business or pleasure?" the clerk asked, glancing at the case.*

*"Both," Arthur said.*

*He meant neither.*

The upper receiver and lower receiver lay disassembled on a hotel towel he'd laid across the writing desk. The towel was white. The components were matte black. The contrast pleased him. Everything in its place. His kit was laid out in order: CLP solvent, bore patches, chamber brush, a small bottle of Slip 2000, picks, dental tools for the hard-to-reach carbon. Everything had been purchased at a hardware store, except the lubricant, which he bought in bulk and decanted into unmarked bottles. He carried nothing that could be traced to a specialty supplier. The rifle itself was unremarkable. A semi-automatic AR platform in .300 Blackout — subsonic capability, short-range work. He'd be inside three hundred meters. Inside the motorcade route, actually, though that was a detail he hadn't been given. He'd done his own recon, as always. The client's recon was a courtesy. Arthur's recon was the law.

The takedown pins were lubed and reinserted. The pivot pin seated with a click. He joined the upper to the lower. The gap was negligible. The rifle was a well-made tool. Nothing more. He found beauty in tools the way a surgeon might find beauty in a scalpel — not in the object, but in the elimination of waste it made possible.

"Security around Aldridge has reportedly been increased following the announcement, with Capitol Police—"

Arthur set the bolt carrier group back into the upper. The charging handle slid home. He pressed the forward assist. It was unnecessary with a clean rifle, but the sound — the metallic snick — settled something inside his chest. A round was not yet chambered. That would come later. Much later. Tuesday morning, in a hotel not this one, in a city he would enter by train.

He wiped down the exterior of the rifle with a dry cloth, removing fingerprints. Not because of this rifle — this one would be destroyed, submerged, dissolved. But because the discipline of wiping was the discipline of existing. A man who left fingerprints was a man who believed he mattered. Arthur did not believe he mattered. He was an intermediary. A routing instruction between a balance sheet and an obituary.

On the television, a photograph of Helena Aldridge appeared. She was smiling. She had a wide, serious face, framed by dark hair streaked with grey. She looked like a librarian, if librarians were privy to classified procurement budgets.

Arthur studied the face for exactly two seconds. Then he muted the television.

He did not need to know her smile.

He folded the towel. He placed the cleaning kit into a leather toiletry bag. The rifle went into a hard case designed for a Stradivarius, a prop he'd used before. A violinist traveling for a concert drew no attention. A man traveling with a rifle case drew every kind.

He checked his watch. 11:47 PM. The news segment was over. They'd moved on to weather, then sports. The world absorbed the detail of Helena Aldridge's planned testimony, chewed on it briefly, and swallowed it. That was how it worked. A person existed, and the world didn't notice. Then the person was gone, and the world didn't notice. The space between those two states was Arthur's province. He lived in the comma between sentences.

He stood and walked to the window. The city below was performing its nightly illusion of permanence — traffic lights cycling, cabs moving, strangers crossing streets in pursuit of other strangers. It all looked so sturdy. So fixed. As if no amount of money could rearrange it.

Arthur knew better. For the right fee, any arrangement was temporary.

He closed the curtains. He checked the deadbolt on the door. He set the alarm on his phone for 5:00 AM. He would need to leave by six. The train to Washington departed at seven-fifteen.

He turned off the lamp.

In the dark, lying on his back above the hotel's duvet, his hands folded on his chest the way they might fold in a casket, Arthur Mendel thought about torque specs, and trigger pull weight, and the trajectory of a .300 AAC Blackout subsonic round at 280 meters, accounting for a five-mile-per-hour crosswind from the east.

He did not think about Helena Aldridge.

He did not think about the fact that she had a daughter, that her husband had died two years ago of lymphoma, that her testimony would never happen, that democracy would continue to creak forward without her voice, that the procurement irregularities would persist beneath new signatures.

These were not his concerns. His concern was windage.

He closed his eyes. He slept the way he worked — precisely, briefly, without interruption.

In five hours, he would wake. The rifle would be clean. The city would still be pretending. And somewhere in Washington, Helena Aldridge would be sleeping too — also above her duvet, also with her hands folded — and she would not know that a man in the next city over had just spent forty minutes preparing the instrument of her erasure with the same tender care a violinist might use to tune the very instrument Arthur's case was built to impersonate.

The world was full of these ironies.

Arthur Mendel did not enjoy them. He didn't dislike them, either.

He simply didn't notice.

He woke at 5:00 AM. The alarm was a single vibration. He packed in eleven minutes. He left the room the way he'd found it — bed made, towels folded, air conditioner humming at sixty-eight degrees. The only evidence he'd been there was a missing bottle of shampoo, which the hotel would not inventory for another three days, and by then the trail would be theoretical, and theoretical trails did not interest anyone.

He carried the violin case to the lobby. The night clerk nodded.

"Business or pleasure?" the clerk asked, glancing at the case.

"Both," Arthur said.

He meant neither.

# Midnight Run

The staging area reeked of high-octane fuel and bad decisions.

Marcus pulled the rubber mask down over his face, the neoprene pressing against his cheekbones, filtering nothing but his own ragged breath. Around him, the outskirts of the city's industrial district hummed with a different kind of electricity tonight — not the steady drone of machinery, but the guttural symphony of engines being revved past their limits.

Forty-seven cars. He'd counted them. Each one a weapon disguised as a hobby, their hoods popped open like gaping mouths, spilling their mechanical guts onto the cracked asphalt of the old container yard. Neon underglow painted the fog in violet and acid green. Somewhere behind the rows of trailers and shipping containers, a bass beat thudded through a speaker system someone had jury-rigged to a generator.

This was the Midnight Run. Invitation only. No GPS coordinates, no paper trails. Just a location dropped to your encrypted chat two hours before, and a buy-in that could buy a decent house in the suburbs. Five hundred thousand on the table tonight. Winner takes all. Second place gets a hospital bill. Everything else — well.

He'd seen the wrecks from previous years. Scraped off the concrete barriers in pieces. The organizers called it "acceptable attrition." The drivers who survived called it something else entirely.

Marcus ran his hand along the driver's side quarter panel of his car — a matte black Nissan Silvia that had cost him three years of dangerous debt and one ex-girlfriend. He'd built her from the chassis up, spending nights in a friend's garage under halogen lights that buzzed like trapped wasps. She wasn't the fastest thing here tonight. Not by a long shot. But she was *his*, and he knew every one of her sounds, her temperaments, her little mechanical lies.

"Silvia's looking good tonight, Park." The voice came from behind him, velvety with condescension.

He turned. Diane Voss leaned against the flatbed of a support truck, arms folded, her custom matte grey Skyline gleaming behind her like a loyal predator. She was the favorite tonight. Three-time champion of the Run. They called her "The Ghost" because she was impossible to follow through the twistbacks.

"Looking's not the same as winning," Marcus said.

Diane smiled — that thin, knowing smile that never reached her eyes. "You're right. It isn't."

She walked away. Her crew fell in behind her, huddled around tablets and walkie-talkies, a whole entourage of mechanics and strategists. Marcus had brought himself. And his car. That was it.

---

The route was always kept secret until thirty minutes before the green flag. That was the deal — you showed up, you saw the map, and you *committed*. No practice runs. No reconnaissance. Just a map projected onto a screen mounted to the side of a rusted-out crane, the red line of the route snaking through the industrial district, past the old shipping canal, and out to the decommissioned highway overpass that served as the finish line.

Sixteen miles. Forty-seven cars. Two lanes of road that barely qualified as road anymore, flanked by concrete Jersey barriers that had absorbed impacts from years of races nobody would ever officially acknowledge.

Marcus studied the route, burning the turns into his memory. Left at the old grain silo. Hard right at the canal bridge. S-curve through the warehouse district. Straightaway along the old rail line. Then the long uphill sweep to the overpass where the finish line waited.

It was the S-curve that worried him. That was where cars died. The barriers narrowed there — someone had explained to him once that it was deliberate, a way to thin the herd. The Run wasn't just about speed. It was about survival.

He walked back to his car and slid into the driver's seat. The familiar smell of worn upholstery and dried sweat from his last track day mixed with the sharper scent of gasoline from the jerry can in his trunk. He pulled his racing gloves on, one finger at a time, and tried to slow his heart rate. It didn't work.

*Focus.*

He checked the gauges. Oil pressure good. Fuel full. The aftermarket racing harness clipped tight across his chest, pressing his shoulders back against the seat. He flexed his fingers on the steering wheel and felt the faint tremor in his hands — not fear exactly, but that electric vibration that comes right before you do something you can't undo.

---

The countdown started. Cars jockeyed for position along the starting line, a jagged row of metal and carbon fiber and pure recklessness. The starter stood on a flatbed trailer, her arm raised, a LED baton in her fist. The crowd pushed against the invisible line of the staging area — faces lit by phone screens and underglow, their voices merging into a wall of noise that Marcus couldn't parse into words anymore.

He didn't want words. He wanted the green.

*Three.*

His right foot feathered the gas. The engine climbed. The vibration traveled through the pedal, through his ankle, through his bones.

*Two.*

His left hand gripped the shifter. His right hand white-knuckled the wheel. The harness dug into his chest.

*One.*

The baton dropped.

---

The first mile was pure chaos. Cars surged forward like animals released from cages, and the noise was beyond anything — a physical thing, a pressure wave that compressed Marcus's chest as engines screamed past six thousand RPM and held. He was in fourteenth off the line, the Silvia's rear end skating on the dusty asphalt as he fought for traction through the first right-hander.

The car ahead of him — a wide-body Supra — drifted wide, and Marcus saw the opening. He buried his right foot, the turbo spooling with that characteristic whistle-whine, and threaded the gap between the Supra and the concrete barrier with what couldn't have been more than eight inches of clearance on either side.

*Twelfth.*

The adrenaline was already hitting. It came like a wave from his gut, up through his chest, and into his temples, a hot rush that made everything simultaneously too sharp and too slow. Time stretched. The world became a series of frames — each one burned into his retinas with terrible clarity. The way a WRX's taillights blurred as he passed it on the canal bridge straight. The wet sheen of the canal water below reflecting neon underglow. The sound of his own breathing, ragged and fast, inside his helmet.

*Ninth.*

By the grain silo, the field had started to thin. Two cars had already gone off — a Civic into the barrier hard enough to trigger the airbag, and a modified Audi that lost a tire on debris and limped into the dirt runoff. The Civic driver was moving — that was all Marcus could tell before he had to look forward again. The Run had its own medical team. They'd handle it. He couldn't afford to stop. Nobody could. That was the deal.

*Sixth.*

The S-curve loomed.

---

The first bend hit like a question. Marcus pitched the Silvia into it, weight shifting, the rear stepping out just enough. Counter-steer. Hold. The barrier was close enough that he could see the concrete texture in his headlights, the old impacts and scarring from races past, each one a small monument to someone's worst night. He held his line and the car gripped, pulling through the first hairpin with the mechanical scream of tires being asked to do something tires were never designed to do.

The second bend tightened. He braked early — he always braked early here — and felt the deceleration pull the harness tight across his collarbones. The pedal felt... different. Slightly soft. He blinked. The car slowed. He released the brakes and the Silvia rotated through the second curve, and he was through the S-curve, the barriers falling away behind him.

*Wait.*

That pedal feel. Soft. Long. He'd felt that a thousand times on the track when the pads got hot. But they shouldn't be hot yet. He hadn't braked hard enough. Had he?

He glanced at the mirror. Four cars behind him. The headlights of the Ghost's Skyline were there, two cold blue eyes in the dark.

*Fourth.*

The straightaway opened up. He pushed the pedal down and the Silvia surged, the boost building. 100. 110. 120. The rail line blurred past on either side, the old tracks running parallel like silver stitches in the earth. Marcus watched the temp gauge. Watched the boost. Watched the road.

*The pedal.*

He pressed the brake lightly. Just a test. Just to check.

The pedal went down.

Far. Too far. It sank almost to the floor before he felt any resistance at all, and even then it was weak — like pressing into wet sand. The car barely slowed.

His stomach dropped. A cold knot tightened just below his ribs.

*No.*

He pumped the pedal. Fast. Hard. The old technique — pump the brakes to build pressure. It worked, barely. The pedal firmed up on the third pump, enough to slow the car from 130 to 110 before it went soft again. But that was wrong. That was all wrong. The pressure wasn't holding. Something was gone.

*They've been cut.*

The thought arrived with the clarity of a knife edge. Someone had been under his car. Someone had opened the bleeder valve on the brake line, or cut the hose, or done something — something quiet, something quick — while he'd been studying the route map and trusting the staging area.

*Diane's smile. That thin, knowing smile that never reached her eyes.*

She had crew. She had people. She'd walked past his car. She'd walked past every car. She'd had time. She'd had *opportunity*.

The cold knot in his stomach turned to ice.

---

*Think. Think. Think.*

The uphill sweep to the overpass was coming. Two miles of rising road with a concrete barrier on the right and a metal guardrail on the left. The finish line was at the top. He was in fourth place. The Skyline was behind him, gaining.

Marcus's mind went white with panic for one electric second. His hands shook. The car was at 115 and the uphill sweep was a long, wide curve, but after that — after the finish line — there was nothing. The overpass ended at a barricade. Concrete and sand-filled barrels and the empty air beyond. If you won, the organizers opened a gate that let you sweep left onto the access road. If you won.

If your brakes didn't work, and you were doing 115, and you couldn't slow down enough to make that left turn —

He'd hit the barricade.

He'd hit it *hard*.

He pumped the pedal again. It caught, barely, and he bled maybe 10 mph off. Down to 105. But it wasn't enough. He needed 30 mph at the top to make the gate. He needed to be at 30 and he was at 105 and the brakes were dying beneath his foot like something bleeding out.

*Engine braking.*

He downshifted. Hard. The transmission protested with a metallic howl, and the revs spiked, and the car lurched as the engine's compression grabbed hold and started dragging the speed down. 95. 90. The Silvia shuddered. The tachometer needle swung into the red.

But it wasn't enough. The overpass was right there. He could see the barrier. The barricade. The sand barrels. The orange reflective tape on the concrete. And beyond it — beyond it was just air and the dark and the canal sixty feet below.

The Skyline was right behind him. Diane's headlights filled his mirror. She wasn't slowing down. She wasn't going to slow down. She knew. She *knew*, and she was going to push him straight into the barricade and take the win.

Marcus made a decision in the space between heartbeats.

He couldn't stop. So he had to steer.

He aimed the Silvia left. At the guardrail. Not head-on — angled. The way you're supposed to hit a guardrail if you ever, God forbid, have to. Glancing. Let the metal absorb the energy in a long scrape instead of a single catastrophic impact.

The guardrail came at him like a wall of light.

The impact wasn't a single moment. It was a *sequence*. First, the sound — a shriek of metal tearing metal that went through his skull like a drill bit. Then the spin. The Silvia hit the guardrail and rotated, and the world became a blur of lights and concrete and sky and concrete again. He felt the harness catch him, felt his neck snap forward and then back, felt the car leave the ground for one horrible weightless second before it came down on its side and slid.

The screech of the guardrail and the crunch of the Silvia's quarter panel folding into the wheel well filled his ears, and then the barrier was gone, and the car was spinning on the asphalt on its wheels, somehow still on its wheels, and then it stopped.

Silence.

Or not silence. His ears were ringing too loudly for silence. But the engine had died, and the world had stopped spinning, and he was sitting in the dark in a car that was tilted at a wrong angle, and the smell of gasoline was everywhere. Thick. Suffocating. The kind of gasoline smell that meant a line had ruptured, that meant fuel was pooling somewhere it shouldn't be, that meant one spark and —

Marcus hit the harness release. It stuck. He hit it again. His hands were shaking so badly he could barely grip the clasp. The third time it released, and the harness fell away, and he threw his shoulder into the door. It opened. He fell out onto the asphalt, and the cold night air hit his face, and he tasted blood where he'd bitten his tongue, and the gasoline smell was even stronger out here, and behind him, distantly, he could hear the Skyline's engine.

Crossing the finish line.

Winner takes all.

---

He lay on his back on the cracked asphalt and stared up at the sky. Stars. Faint through the light pollution, but there. The adrenaline was still screaming through his veins, and his hands wouldn't stop trembling, and his breath came in shallow, fast gulps that made black spots swim at the edges of his vision.

The Silvia leaked fuel in a dark, spreading pool that caught the reflection of distant headlights. He could hear people running. Shouting. The medical team, probably. Or the organizers. Or both.

He thought about the pedal. The soft, sinking pedal. The way it had gone to the floor. The way it had felt like betrayal.

He thought about Diane's smile.

That thin, knowing smile.

He closed his eyes and felt the cold asphalt against his back and listened to the gasoline drip and the shouting grow closer and the Skyline's engine fade into the distance.

He'd fix the brakes.

And then he'd see her at the next Run.
