# Block D

The first signal was the lights.

Every bulb in Block D died at 7:42 PM, and the darkness hit like a held breath. Then the screaming started—not the usual shouting, not the territorial posturing that the guards had learned to tune out. This was something else entirely. This was the sound of a dam breaking.

Someone had gotten to the panel box. That much was clear. What wasn't clear yet—not to the officers on the tier, not to the control room staring at dead camera feeds—was that two guards had been pulled into Cell 14 during the thirty seconds of confusion that followed the blackout.

Sergeant Reeves was the first to respond, keying his radio with one hand and drawing his baton with the other. "Control, Block D, we have a situation—" The radio gave back nothing but static. They'd jammed the frequency somehow, or smashed the repeater. Reeves didn't get to find out which. A bedsheet rope dropped over the railing from the second tier and caught him around the throat from behind. He was still clawing at it when they dragged him over the edge.

---

The riot didn't spread so much as *erupt* simultaneously. That was the terrifying part, the part that would later suggest weeks of planning. Cells opened in clusters—not all at once, which would have triggered the automated lockdown, but in a staggered sequence that the system's logic read as a series of individual malfunctions. By the time anyone in the control room understood what they were seeing, forty inmates were loose on the ground floor and more were coming down the stairs.

Marcus Cole, serving life for three counts of murder, moved through the chaos with a purpose that separated him from the pack. While others screamed and smashed, he walked directly toward the guard station at the end of the corridor. He carried a shank—eight inches of sharpened bed frame, wrapped at the handle with torn bedsheets—and he didn't wave it around or threaten with it. He simply used it. The guard behind the station, a man named Patterson who was three years from retirement, barely got his hand up before Cole was past him and into the control room.

That was when the cell doors on the segregation unit opened too.

---

Officer Diana Torres had been on the job for eleven months. She'd done the training, watched the videos, sat through the seminars on riot response. None of it had included what to do when you were locked in a supply closet with three inmates between you and the only exit, and your pepper spray had already been used—emptied into the face of the first one, who'd barely flinched before grabbing her wrist and twisting until something in her forearm made a sound like a branch snapping.

She backed up until her shoulders hit the shelving unit behind her. Cleaning supplies clattered to the floor. The inmate with the pepper-sprayed face was wiping his eyes with his shirt, but the other two were advancing. One held a length of pipe torn from the plumbing access panel. The other had nothing in his hands, which was somehow worse.

"Come on, baby," the unarmed one said. "We just wanna talk."

Torres grabbed a bottle of industrial degreaser from the shelf behind her and held it like a weapon. Her broken forearm throbbed with every heartbeat. The fluorescent emergency lighting—battery-backed, dim, casting everything in a sick amber—made the men's faces look like something out of a nightmare.

She threw the degreaser into the unarmed man's eyes and ran for the door. She made it four steps into the corridor before the pipe caught her behind the knee.

---

On the second tier, a group of Aryan Brotherhood members had taken control of the east wing with military precision. They'd fashioned shields from mattress covers stretched over table legs, and they moved in a tight formation that pushed everything before them—other inmates who weren't part of their crew, guards who'd been caught in the open. One guard, a young man named Kowalski who'd started that month, was surrounded near the stairwell. He was on the ground in a fetal position when they reached him. What happened next took less than thirty seconds and would be described in the subsequent investigation as "a sustained group assault resulting in catastrophic injuries."

The investigation report would be clinical. The reality was not.

---

In the control room, Cole sat in the captain's chair and studied the monitors. Most were dead, but three still showed feeds—one from the yard, one from the intake area, and one from the infirmary. He could see inmates moving through the corridors below, could see the flicker of fires being set in cells. Someone had gotten into the kitchen. Smoke was beginning to curl under doorframes.

He picked up the landline—the hardwired one that didn't rely on the radio system—and found it dead. They'd cut the lines. Of course they had. He'd planned for that too.

What Cole hadn't planned for was the tactical response team arriving in under eight minutes. The prison's silent alarm—a hardwired system independent of the radio and computer networks—had triggered the moment the segregation doors opened. The state police barracks was four miles away.

The first flashbang came through the window of the control room at 7:53 PM, eleven minutes after the lights went out. Cole didn't even have time to cover his ears.

---

By 8:30, it was over in the sense that the tactical team had secured the main corridors and the control room. It was not over in the sense that cells throughout the block still held inmates who refused to come out, who had fashioned barricades and weapons and hostages. The negotiation team wouldn't arrive until midnight. In the meantime, the smoke from the kitchen fires spread through the ventilation system, and the inmates in the sealed cells on the third tier began to cough.

Two guards were dead. One would die in surgery at 3:17 AM. Fourteen others were injured, six critically. Three inmates were dead—two killed by the tactical team, one killed by other inmates in what appeared to be a settling of old scores carried out under cover of the chaos. The final injury count for inmates would reach thirty-one.

Sergeant Reeves survived. He was found in Cell 14, conscious, with a fractured vertebra and a concussion. He would not return to work.

Officer Torres survived as well, though she would require three surgeries to repair her arm and would carry a limp for the rest of her life from the damage done by the pipe.

The investigation would take fourteen months. The report would fill nine hundred pages. It would identify systemic failures, staffing shortages, intelligence lapses, and infrastructure decay. It would make forty-seven recommendations.

Block D would remain closed for two years.

---

In the aftermath, when they reviewed the footage from the one working camera in the yard, they would see Marcus Cole stepping out of the control room into the corridor at 7:51 PM—two minutes before the flashbang came through the window. He'd known the tactical team was coming. He'd always known. The riot, the deaths, the destruction—none of it had been the point.

The point had been Cell 9, Segregation Unit, where a man named David Liu was being held pending transfer to federal custody. Liu had testified against people who had long memories and deep resources.

When they found Liu's cell, the door was open and the man was gone.

The riot had never been a riot at all. It had been a extraction.

# Room Service

The Economy Inn on Route 9 smelled like mildrew and industrial cleaner. Marcus ran a patch down the barrel of his Glock, holding it up to the lamp light like a jeweler inspecting a diamond.

"You know what I don't get?" He squinted through the barrel. "Poison people."

Sitting cross-legged on the other bed, Delia oiled the slide of her SIG Sauer with a rag, not looking up. "What about it?"

"It's impersonal. You might as well be an accountant. Where's the craft?"

Delia laughed, a short, dry sound. "Craft. Listen to you. Since when is this a trade guild?"

"I'm serious. Anybody can slip something in a drink. A *child* could do that."

"A child doesn't have access to tetrodotoxin."

"You know what I mean." Marcus reassembled the slide with practiced hands. "There's no skill in it. No timing. You just—what—wait around?"

"That's exactly the skill." Delia set down the SIG and picked up a smaller piece, a Walther PPK, field-stripped on the towel like a tiny surgery. "The waiting is the whole point. You have to control every variable. What they eat, when they eat, who prepares it. You have to understand the target's *entire day*. It's the most personal method there is."

"It's the most *boring* method there is."

"You once told me your preferred method was 'defenestration.' You literally just push someone out a window."

Marcus pointed the cleaning rod at her. "First of all, it's not *just* pushing. You have to get them to the window. That takes setup. Subtlety. And second—there's something honest about it. Gravity does the work, but *you* made the choice. Face to face."

"Most of your targets are on the fourteenth floor, Marcus. That's not intimacy. That's real estate."

"Yeah?"

"I know. Clean shot. Base of the skull."

"Tap here twice first. So I know it's coming."

"That defeats the purpose."

"I know."

He dialed. She closed her eyes.

# The Pyre

The first torch kiss was almost gentle.

Heat licked the kindling at her bare feet, and for a moment it was merely warmth—a summer hearth, a baking stone, the kind of heat that makes you drowsy. Then the dry straw caught. Then the brush. Then the crossbeams.

The heat stopped being warmth and became *pressure*.

It rose through her, and the air itself turned thick, turned visible, turned into something she could taste—bitter, resiny, choking. Her skin tightened across her hands and face. Sweat evaporated before it could form. The ropes binding her wrists to the post grew hot against her skin, then hotter, then they *seared*, and she twisted against them with nowhere to go.

The smoke came in slow coils at first, gray and lazy, then black and rolling. It pooled at her feet and climbed her body like a living thing. She held her breath. She held it until her lungs screamed and her vision swam, and then she gasped, and the smoke rushed in—hot, acrid, filling her, coating her throat in soot and ash. She coughed. The coughing made her inhale deeper. The deeper she inhaled, the more smoke replaced air.

Above, the sky was a pale blue she remembered from childhood. It remained indifferent.

The crowd watched. Some faces were grim. Some were eager. A woman near the front was weeping, though whether for her or for the spectacle, she couldn't tell. The magistrate's lips moved, but the words were just sounds now—Latin or prayer or accusation, it no longer mattered.

The pain arrived in stages.

First, the blistering. Her feet and shanks, where the fire ate closest, bloomed with welts that burst and wept and dried instantly in the heat. Then the deeper pain beneath—nerve endings screaming, then going silent in patches as feeling fled. The silence of deadened flesh was worse than the pain, because it meant the fire had reached a place it could not return from.

She opened her mouth to pray and smoke poured in instead.

What came out was not a prayer. It was not a curse. It was not the defiant declaration she had rehearsed in her cell through the long nights before. It was simply sound—the raw, guttural noise of a body that had passed beyond language, beyond thought, beyond anything but the single, overwhelming fact of its own destruction.

The first scream was high and thin, a sound like a kettle, like something small and trapped. The second was lower, rougher, torn from somewhere deeper in the chest. The third was hardly human at all.

Somewhere in the crowd, someone vomited. Someone else looked away. A child asked a question and was hushed.

The screaming did not stop so much as *change*—rising in pitch, breaking apart, becoming something fragmented and wet, until finally, mercifully, the smoke took her voice entirely.

The pyre popped and settled. Sparks rose in a column toward that pale, indifferent sky.

The crowd waited for the ashes to cool before they would even know what was left.

---

*Written as historical/literary fiction. The burning of accused "witches" was a real and devastating historical tragedy that claimed tens of thousands of lives, predominantly women, across Europe and the Americas.*

# The Awakening

The language was not meant for human mouths.

Kaelast knew this as the syllables tore free from his throat — wet, guttural things that seemed to squirm in the air like severed tongues still twitching with life. He stood at the center of the battlefield, where the dead lay stacked three deep in places, a carpet of ruin stretching beneath a sky the color of a bruise. The blood in the soil was still warm. That mattered. Death was freshest here, and fresher was always easier.

Easier. Not *right*.

He felt the magic pool in his chest like swallowed tar — dense, cold, and slow. It did not flow the way fire magic flowed, or the way healing knit itself through the body in threads of warm light. This *pushed*. It pushed downward through his ribs, through his stomach, through his legs, into the earth, and where it touched the dead, it *insisted*.

The first hand broke the surface.

It came up wrong — not clawing, not desperate, but with the slow, patient certainty of something that had forgotten what urgency meant. The fingers were partially skeletonized, tendons hanging like stripped sinew from a butcher's hook, and they flexed with a sound like wet rope tightening. Kaelast watched the hand plant itself against the mud, and he felt a flicker of revulsion that he had long since learned to swallow.

Then another hand. Another. Dozens. Then hundreds.

They rose like wheat in reverse, these things that had once been men. A soldier in a corroded breastplate pulled himself free from the muck, and half his face sloughed away as he emerged — the skin separating from the muscle beneath with a soft, organic tearing, like bark peeling from a dead oak. His jaw hung loose on one side, a single tendon keeping it from swinging freely, and his eyes — God, his *eyes* — were not empty. They were filled with something. Not life. Not thought. But a pale, milky awareness, like a sleeper caught between dreaming and waking who knows only that they are no longer at rest.

Kaelast could feel them. That was the worst of it.

The magic created a tether — not control, exactly, but *awareness*. He could feel every one of them as a cold point against his consciousness, like being touched by a hundred frostbitten fingers simultaneously. And through that tether, he could feel what they felt: a dim, aching *wrongness*. They knew, on some level deeper than thought, that they were not supposed to be standing. Their bodies screamed the truth in a language below language — that flesh should rest, that bone should lie still, that the dead had earned their silence.

He had stolen it from them.

A woman rose near his left foot, her throat opened so wide that her head lolled to one side at an angle that made Kaelast's own neck ache in sympathy. Blackened blood still crusted the wound, and when she breathed in — because the magic *made* them breathe, that was part of the wrongness, the insistence on mimicking the mechanics of the living — the air whistled through the gap in her neck with a sound like a child blowing across a bottle top.

She turned her head toward him. The loll worsened. Her eyes found his.

He looked away.

More now. The field was *breathing* with movement. Corpses hauling themselves upright with shattered legs, femurs grinding against pelvises with a sound like wooden dowels snapping. One man rose with a spear still buried in his chest, the shaft bobbing gently with each movement, and Kaelast could see the wood had begun to rot from the inside where the death-magic touched it. Another dragged itself forward on its arms alone, its lower body a ruin of churned tissue and exposed spine, the vertebrae clicking against one another like rosary beads.

The smell hit him then.

He had been so focused on the incantation, on maintaining the tether, that he hadn't noticed it building — a wall of sweet, thick rot that coated the back of his throat like grease. It was the smell of things decomposing *and not finished decomposing*, of bodies caught in a stasis that was neither decay nor preservation, but some third, hideous state that had no name because nature had never intended for it to exist.

Kaelast gagged, and the magic flickered.

A hundred dead eyes turned toward him at once.

He steadied himself. Steadied the tether. The magic settled back into its rhythm — that terrible, insistent *push* — and the army turned as one to face the horizon, where the distant glow of the living city still burned against the darkening sky.

"Walk," Kaelast said.

His voice sounded very small against the silence of a thousand dead things waiting for his command.

And then they walked.

The air in the subterranean garage was thick with the smell of stale oil, damp concrete, and the sharp, metallic tang of fear. Around the perimeter, shadows shifted—the silent, watchful forms of the Syndicate’s upper echelon. In the center of the concrete floor, illuminated by a single swinging halogen bulb, stood eighteen-year-old Marcus. 

Across from him, slumped in a bolted steel chair, was the reason his hands wouldn’t stop shaking. The man was a low-level dealer from a rival turf, his face bruised and swollen, his wrists bound behind the chair with heavy zip ties. He was breathing in wet, ragged gasps, his head lolling forward.

From the darkness, Silas emerged. The leader of the Syndicate was not a large man, but he moved with the unhurried confidence of an apex predator. He circled Marcus like a shark, hands in the pockets of his tailored coat, his eyes assessing the boy’s trembling shoulders and pale face.

"You said you wanted family, Marcus," Silas murmured, his voice echoing softly in the cavernous space. "You said you’d do anything for the block. Anything for the colors."

"I did," Marcus whispered, his throat dry. "I will."

"Words," Silas said, stopping directly in front of Marcus. He tapped the boy’s chest. "They cost nothing. Out here, loyalty isn't a word you say. It’s a debt you pay. In blood."

Silas snapped his fingers. From the shadows stepped Torres, Silas’s chief enforcer, a wall of a man with dead, unblinking eyes. Torres held out a heavy, lead-weighted blackjacking bat. The wood was wrapped in fraying black tape, the end stained a dull, dark crimson. 

Marcus stared at the weapon. He didn't want to touch it. 

"Take it," Silas commanded, his tone dropping a degree colder. The garage seemed to shrink. The ring of gang members stepped closer, their collective breath a low, rumbling pressure in the dark. Marcus could feel their eyes on him. If he turned and ran, he wouldn't make it three steps. 

"Silas, he doesn't know anything," Marcus pleaded, nodding toward the bound man. "He's nobody. I can run product, I can watch the corners—"

"You do what you're told," Silas interrupted, stepping so close that Marcus could smell the menthols on his breath. "You think we let people wear our patch just because they’re good at running? Anyone can run. We need to know that when the time comes, you won't freeze. We need to know you're broken in."

Silas gripped the back of Marcus’s neck, his fingers like iron clamps, forcing the boy to look at the beaten man. 

"If that bat doesn't swing, Marcus, the next one will swing at you. And we don't stop at bruises." Silas leaned into his ear. "Prove you're one of us. Break him."

The pressure was a physical weight, crushing the air from Marcus’s lungs. He looked at the bat. He looked at the rival. The man lifted his head, his eyes swollen shut, blood streaming from a split lip. "Please," the man wheezed, coughing up a spray of red. "I got kids..."

Marcus squeezed his eyes shut. He thought of his mother, of the eviction notice on their door. He thought of the respect the Syndicate commanded, the safety their numbers provided. He thought of what Torres would do to him if he failed.

He took the bat. It was heavier than he thought. 

"Open your eyes," Silas hissed. "You look away, we start over."

Marcus forced his eyes open. The halogen bulb swung, casting long, stark shadows. The gang watched in absolute, breathless silence. They wanted to see the boy die, and they wanted to see the monster be born.

Marcus raised the bat. His arms felt like they were filled with wet sand. He tightened his grip until his knuckles turned white, his breath hitching in his chest. 

Silas nodded once. "Do it."

Marcus swung. The impact was a sickening, dense *thud* that vibrated violently up the wood and into his shoulders, rattling his teeth. The man let out a guttural, broken shriek that bounced off the concrete walls. Marcus stumbled back, the bat suddenly feeling like it weighed a hundred pounds.

# The Last Course

The candlelight caught the rim of his wine glass beautifully. I had always admired that about Martin — his taste in glassware, if nothing else.

"You're quiet tonight," he said, cutting into the risotto. I watched the fork travel upward. Watched his jaws work. Watched him swallow.

"Just savoring it," I said. I meant more than the food.

He laughed. Martin always laughed easily. It was one of the things I'd once found charming about him. Now it simply confirmed what I already knew — that he never looked closely enough at anything. Not at his business partners. Not at his wife. Not at the woman across the table who had stirred dried foxglove into his stock with the care of a chemist.

"This is exceptional," he said, taking another bite. "Really, Eleanor. You've outdone yourself."

"Thank you. It's an old family recipe."

That much was true, in its way. My grandmother had known the gardens well. She had taught me that the line between medicine and poison was merely a question of dosage and intention. Digitalis purpurea. Beautiful trumpet-shaped flowers, purple and white. In the right quantity, it strengthened the heart. In a larger quantity, it confused it utterly.

I had measured carefully.

Martin reached for his wine. "The Whitmore contract came through today," he said, his voice carrying that particular self-satisfaction I had grown to despise over three years of partnership and betrayal. "They accepted the revised terms. Every clause."

"How wonderful for you," I said.

He didn't catch the emphasis. He never did.

I lifted my own fork and ate from my plate — the same risotto, prepared from the same pot. I had been careful about that. There was a certain poetry in eating the same meal, a kind of communion. I had simply prepared my portion first, before I had reached for the small mahogany box I kept on the top shelf of the pantry, behind the saffron.

The first quarter hour passed in comfortable silence, or what Martin took for comfortable silence. He spoke about the merger. He spoke about the vacation he was planning — Sicily in the autumn, he thought. He asked if I'd ever been.

"Once," I said. "A long time ago."

He was halfway through his second helping when I noticed the first subtle shift. A momentary pause between sentences. His hand drifted to his chest — not dramatically, not with any sense of alarm, but with the absent gesture of a man who feels something slightly unusual and dismisses it.

"Heartburn," he muttered, more to himself than to me. He took another sip of wine.

"Perhaps the risotto is richer than you're accustomed to," I offered.

"Perhaps." He smiled, but it was thinner now. A fissure in the plaster.

I had read everything I could find. The onset was variable. Sometimes forty minutes. Sometimes two hours. I had timed the meal accordingly — a slow evening, candles lit, music playing softly from the speaker in the corner. Chopin's Nocturnes. It seemed appropriate. Martin had always preferred something he called "ambiance," though I suspected he couldn't tell Chopin from a commercial jingle.

Twenty minutes later, he set down his fork.

"Eleanor, I feel —" He paused. Blinked. "I feel rather strange."

"Strange how?"

My voice was perfectly calibrated. Concerned. Surprised. The voice of a friend who cannot imagine what might be wrong.

He pressed his palm flat against his sternum. "My heart. It's — racing. Then it slows down. Then it races again." He laughed, but there was no humor in it. "Must be the wine. I shouldn't have had so much on an empty —"

He stopped. His pupils were dilating unevenly. I noticed it clearly in the candlelight — one slightly wider than the other, like a door left ajar.

"Martin, you've gone pale. Should I call someone?"

"No. No, I just need to —" He pushed his chair back. The legs scraped against the tile with a sound like a held breath releasing. He stood, swayed, and gripped the edge of the table. The wine glass trembled. A bead of crimson slid down the stem.

"I think I need to sit down," he said, though he was already standing. The confusion in his voice was delicate, almost dreamlike.

"Let me help you to the sofa."

I rose and guided him by the elbow. He was heavier than I expected, and his arm beneath my hand was rigid, trembling with a fine vibration. I could feel his pulse through the fabric of his shirt — irregular, stumbling over itself like a runner tripping on a root. Fast. Slow. Fast. A rhythm that had lost its reason.

We reached the sofa. He collapsed more than sat. His head fell back against the cushion, and his eyes found the ceiling.

"Something's wrong," he said. The words were slightly blurred now, arriving a half-beat behind his lips. "Something's really wrong, Eleanor."

I knelt beside him. I could have been a Madonna in a painting — the devoted companion, the kneeling witness, the face of gentle alarm.

"I'm going to call an ambulance," I said, with the precise intonation of someone who absolutely was not going to call an ambulance.

"Yes," he whispered. "Please."

His breathing had changed. Shallow, then deep, then shallow again, as though his lungs couldn't decide on a pattern. A sheen of sweat had appeared along his hairline, and his lips — I noticed this with the detachment of a naturalist observing a specimen — had taken on a faint blue tinge at the edges. Cyanosis. The heart was faltering, and the blood was no longer carrying its cargo of oxygen to the places that needed it most.

"Eleanor." His hand found my wrist. His grip was weaker than it should have been. "The Whitmore contract. I need to tell you —"

"Shh. Save your strength."

"I need to tell you — I changed the terms. After the — after you signed. I moved your — your shares into —"

"I know," I said.

His eyes found mine. And in that moment, through the gathering fog of his failing body, I watched understanding arrive. It came slowly, like a figure emerging from mist. First confusion. Then recognition. Then something that was not quite fear and not quite surprise, but a kind of terrible, delayed clarity — the look of a man who has finally, too late, begun to pay attention.

"You," he said.

I said nothing. I simply stayed where I was, kneeling beside him, holding his hand as it loosened its grip on my wrist. The Chopin continued from the speaker — the Nocturne in E-flat major, if I remembered correctly. A piece about tenderness and loss. I had always thought it was rather perfect.

His breathing slowed further. His eyes remained open, fixed on something beyond the ceiling, beyond the room. His heart — that faithless, faithful organ — stuttered one last time, like a clock winding down, and was still.

I remained kneeling for several minutes. The candle on the table guttered in a draft I hadn't noticed before. The risotto cooled in its dish. Somewhere outside, a car passed, its headlights sweeping briefly across the wall.

I stood, smoothed my skirt, and began to clear the table.

I washed the dishes by hand, as I always did. I dried them and returned them to their proper places. I wiped down the counter, the stove, the cutting board. I returned the saffron to its shelf, and I returned the small mahogany box to its place beside it.

Then I poured myself a glass of the remaining wine — the same bottle, the same vintage Martin had been drinking — and I sat in the chair opposite the sofa, and I drank it slowly, in silence, watching the candles burn lower.

He had been right about one thing. It was an exceptional meal.

# The Plank

The deck fell silent as two burly crewmen dragged Elias Mercer from the hold, his wrists bound before him with tarred rope. The morning sun beat down mercilessly on the *Crimson Hart*, and every soul aboard knew what came next.

Captain Sable stood at the starboard rail, arms folded, her weathered face betraying nothing. A plank — ten feet of warped oak — had been extended over the water, lashed to the gunwale. Below, the Caribbean churnred an unsettling shade of steel blue.

"Mercer," Sable said, her voice carrying across the deck like a blade. "You swore an oath before God and this crew. You broke it."

"She's lying!" Mercer thrashed against the men holding him. "I never conspired with—"

"Silence." Sable nodded toward the water. "The fins have been circling since dawn. Nature provides, Mercer. Even justice does."

Elias looked over the rail and felt his stomach drop. Three dark shapes — no, four — cut lazy figure-eights beneath the surface, their dorsal fins breaking the water with mechanical precision. Reef sharks, drawn by the offal the cook had been tossing overboard for an hour on Sable's orders.

"Please," Mercer whispered. His legs buckled. The crewmen hauled him upright. "I have a son in Port Royal. He's only six. *Please.*"

Sable's jaw tightened, but she did not waver. "Should have thought of the boy before you tried to poison my rum." She gestured to the plank. "Walk."

They marched him to the edge. His bare feet — they'd taken his boots — touched the sun-warmed wood. He looked down. The water seemed impossibly far and impossibly close at once.

"I can't," he breathed.

"Then I'll push you, and you'll go in sideways. Your choice."

Mercer shuffled forward. One step. Two. The plank groaned beneath his weight. Three steps. The ship's rail was behind him now. Open air on every side. The ocean swelled and retreated beneath him, and each time it pulled back, he could see them more clearly — grey bodies, blunt snouts, black eyes like polished stones.

Four steps. The end of the plank.

He stopped. His bound hands trembled violently. Tears cut channels through the grime on his face. He turned back toward the deck, toward the crew — men he'd shared rum with, diced with, sung shanties with in the fo'c'sle. Not one would meet his eye.

"Give my boy my name," he said. "Tell him his father—"

The boatswain's staff caught him between the shoulder blades.

He screamed the whole way down.

The impact knocked the air from his lungs. Salt water flooded his nose and mouth. He thrashed, kicking blindly, his bound hands useless before him. For one desperate moment, he broke the surface, gasped, and felt something brush his leg — rough, like wet sandpaper stretched over iron.

Then the first one hit him.

It took his left side just below the ribs, and the force of it drove him under. He felt pressure — impossible, crushing pressure — and then a tearing that was almost worse in its numbness than the pain that followed like a thunderclap. The water around him darkened. He screamed underwater and bubbles erupted from his mouth.

He surfaced once more, somehow, and the crew saw his face — white, eyes wide and sightless with shock, mouth open in a soundless howl. Blood painted the water in a spreading crimson bloom. Two more sharks closed in. One seized his thigh. The other clamped onto his shoulder and rolled, and the spinning motion pulled him under again.

The thrashing lasted perhaps thirty seconds. Then there was only the churning red water, the grey shapes converging, and the slow, awful stillness that followed.

Silence on deck.

Sable turned from the rail. "Clean the plank," she said to no one in particular. "And someone get that blood out of the scuppers before it rusts the iron."

She descended to her cabin and closed the door.

Behind her, the sharks fed, and the Caribbean swallowed everything.

# The Weight of Her

The first night, it was just the smell.

Marla noticed it around midnight—a faint sweetness beneath the stale air of her apartment, like gardenias left too long in vase water. She checked the kitchen. Checked the trash. Sprayed disinfectant until her eyes burned and her throat tasted like chemicals and lies.

By three in the morning, the smell was everywhere. In her pillow. In her hair. Under her fingernails, as though she'd clawed it up from the earth herself.

She had buried Denise six feet deep in the wet woods behind the reservoir. She was certain of this. She remembered the labor of it—the rocks, the roots, the way the shovel had rattled against stone and sent vibrations up through her wrists and into her teeth. She remembered the rain starting just as she finished, as though the sky had been waiting, holding its breath, watching.

She remembered Denise's face before the dark took it.

She tried not to remember that part.

---

The second night, the tapping started.

It came from the bathroom mirror. A slow, deliberate rhythm—not the erratic knocking of pipes, but something intentional. *Patient.* Three taps. A pause. Three taps. A pause. Marla sat rigid on the edge of her bed, her toes curling against the cold floor, and counted along without meaning to.

When she finally worked up the courage to look, the mirror was fogged from the inside, as though someone had been breathing on the other side of the glass. She wiped it with her sleeve and saw only herself—pale, hollowed, her eyes bruised with sleeplessness.

But her reflection didn't blink when she blinked.

She stumbled backward. The mirror cleared. Her reflection matched her perfectly again, gap-mouthed and trembling.

"You're tired," she told herself. "You haven't slept. You're just tired."

The tapping continued behind her, steady as a heartbeat, until dawn.

---

By the fourth day, the hallucinations had stopped hiding.

Marla saw Denise in the grocery store, standing at the end of the cereal aisle in the same blue dress she'd been wearing when Marla hit her with the tire iron. The dress was wrong, though—soaked through, clinging to her body, dripping a dark trail down the linoleum that no one else seemed to notice. Her hair was matted to her skull, and her jaw hung slightly open, displaced, resting at an angle that living jaws don't permit.

Marla dropped a box of granola and gripped the shelf. A stock boy asked if she was okay. She pointed a shaking finger at the end of the aisle.

There was no one there. Just a wet spot on the floor that could have been anything.

That night, Denise sat at the foot of Marla's bed.

She didn't speak. She didn't need to. She just sat there, her hands folded in her lap, water pooling beneath her on the sheets. Her skin had gone the gray-green of deep water, and her eyes—God, her eyes—were clouded over, milky, like the eyes of a fish on ice. But somehow Marla could feel her *looking*. Could feel that blind gaze pressing into her chest like a thumb against a bruise.

"I didn't mean to," Marla whispered. "You have to understand. I didn't *mean* to."

Denise tilted her head. The movement was wrong—too far, too smooth, like a doll's head on a loose neck. And then she smiled, and her teeth were full of reservoir mud.

Marla screamed until her voice cracked, and when she opened her eyes, the bed was empty. But the sheets were soaked, and they smelled like gardenias and wet earth and something else, something underneath—copper and rot, the secret perfume of decomposition.

She burned the sheets. She couldn't burn the smell.

---

A week passed, and the walls began to breathe.

At least, that's what Marla told herself—that the walls were breathing, that the ceiling was pressing lower each night, that the apartment was *alive* and swallowing her slowly. It was better than the alternative. The alternative was that *she* was the one changing, that her mind was a house with a rotting foundation, and every hour another floorboard gave way.

She stopped eating. Food tasted like silt. She stopped showering because the water felt wrong on her skin—too heavy, too cold, carrying a current that hadn't been in the pipes. She'd stand in the tub and feel it pulling at her ankles, tugging, as though the drain led somewhere deeper than the sewer.

The worst were the moments of clarity.

In the afternoons sometimes, the fog would lift and Marla would see her apartment clearly—the unwashed dishes, the wilted plant on the windowsill, the ordinary mess of a life—and she would understand, with a terrible precision, exactly what she had done. She had taken a woman's life. She had extinguished Denise—the way Denise laughed too loud at bad jokes, the way she always ordered the same coffee, the way she had a mother who called every Sunday and was now calling a number that rang and rang and rang into an empty apartment where a phone sat on a counter beside a wilting plant.

Marla would feel the weight of it then—not metaphorically, but *physically*, a pressure on her chest and shoulders, as though Denise's body had been laid across her own. She would gasp and writhe beneath an invisible corpse, sobbing into hands that still felt the vibration of the tire iron connecting with bone, that remembered how the sound had traveled up through the metal handle and into her wrists, a dull, wet thud that didn't sound the way it does in movies, that sounded *final* in a way no other sound ever had.

And then the fog would return, and Denise would be standing in the corner again, dripping, smiling with her muddy teeth, and Marla would almost be grateful.

At least the ghost didn't make her think.

---

On the eleventh night, Marla found her own grave.

She didn't go looking for it. She woke standing in the woods behind the reservoir, barefoot in the mud, the rain slashing down around her. She had no memory of leaving the apartment. Her feet were cut—she could feel the cuts, the sting of them—but the blood washed away as fast as it came, and when she looked down, the mud in front of her had been *dug up*.

Not Denise's grave. She could see that, still mounded, still undisturbed, ten yards to her left.

This was a new hole. Fresh. Perfectly sized for a woman curled into herself.

Denise stood on the other side of it, holding a shovel.

Her lips moved, but the words didn't come from her mouth. They came from the trees, from the rain, from inside Marla's own skull—a voice that sounded like drowning, like mud filling a throat, like the last wet sound a person makes before the world goes quiet.

*"Get in."*

Marla fell to her knees. The mud soaked through her clothes. She could feel the grave beside her, could feel Denise beneath the ground—not dead, not sleeping, but *waiting*, the way things wait when they have all the time in the world and nothing left to lose.

"I'm sorry," Marla said, and the words were so small they dissolved before they left her mouth. "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry—"

The shovel clattered to the ground.

When the police found her the next morning, she was lying in the mud beside Denise's grave, scratching at the earth with her bare hands, weeping, trying to dig her way down to a woman she could not reach.

They said she was whispering the same thing over and over, her voice raw and ruined:

*"She won't let me in. She won't let me in. She won't let me in."*

They took her to the hospital. They sedated her. They closed her eyes.

But Marla didn't sleep.

Behind her eyelids, the reservoir stretched out black and endless, and somewhere in its depths, Denise was smiling, her muddy teeth gleaming in the dark, her blind eyes finally, finally seeing.

# The Body

The apartment smelled like the city's dying breath — that sweet rot that crawls up from the storm drains in August and settles into the walls like it pays rent.

She was on the floor. What was left of her.

The blood had gone brown at the edges, creeping outward in a shape that reminded me of the harbor on a foggy night — spreading thin where it shouldn't, pooling thick where the floorboards dipped. Her skin had already started losing its argument with gravity, going slack around the jaw the way the old theater on Lexington forgot how to hold its own marquee. One eye still open, watching the ceiling like it might confess something. The other had already surrendered.

I'd seen dead before. Dead is a cocktail napkin sketch. This was a fresco.

Someone had worked on her the way rust works on the el tracks — patient, thorough, starting at the edges and eating inward toward something structural. The cuts weren't rage. Rage is sloppy, starts in one place and panics to the next. These had rhythm. These had a craftsman's quiet obsession, the kind of attention this city used to give to things before it forgot how to care about anything but the price per square foot.

Her fingers were curled the way the weeds curl through cracked concrete on Ashland — gripping nothing, growing toward nothing, just the reflex of something that stopped being alive before it got the message.

I lit a cigarette. The match flame wavered like the last streetlight on a block nobody walks down anymore.

The apartment was the kind of place that had given up expecting anything from anybody. Peeling wallpaper like dead skin on a sunburned shoulder. A radiator clanking its last confession to nobody in particular. The window looked out on an airshaft where the brick was crumbling soft and green, the way teeth go green in the coroner's drawer when the enamel finally quits its post.

She was young once. That much the photographs on the wall testified to — a girl who smiled like the lakefront before the factories closed, before the money left and took the shoreline with it. Now she was just another piece of urban blight nobody with any authority would claim responsibility for. Another vacancy the landlord would fill by Friday.

I crouched beside her. Close enough to see where the knife had done its dissertation on human anatomy. Close enough to smell that her perfume was still fighting the rot and losing, the way the last mom-and-pop on Western fights the coming condo development — brave, pointless, already written into the ledger as a loss.

That's when I noticed her hands. Dirt under the nails. Not potting soil. Not garden variety grime. The kind of dirt that gets under there when you're clawing at something. Crawling. Trying to get away or trying to get *to* something.

The dead don't dig.

Which meant she'd been alive for at least part of this. Alive and trying, the way this whole stupid city keeps trying — scrabbling at the concrete, reaching for something softer underneath, refusing to understand that the concrete always wins.

It always wins.

I stood up. My knees cracked like the sidewalk outside the old Polish church on Division, the one the diocese sold to developers who promised to "preserve the character" before they knocked it flat for parking.

The patrol cop at the door looked green. Fresh badge, soft eyes, still believing that the dead stay neatly in their photographs and the guilty come with identifying markers.

"You got anything?" he asked.

I looked at her one more time. At the way the shadows were already eating her outline, dissolving her into the geography of the floor like rain dissolves a chalk outline — slow, inevitable, the city reclaiming what was always technically its property.

"Yeah," I said. "I got that she knew him."

"How do you figure?"

I pointed to the door. "No forced entry. Lock's clean. She opened it for somebody."

The kid cop frowned. "Could've been a boyfriend. A neighbor. A—"

"Could've been," I said. "But it wasn't. You don't let a stranger in when you're a woman alone in this city. Not this city. Not at 2 AM. Not unless you already stopped being afraid of them."

I took a drag and watched the smoke climb toward the ceiling like the last prayer in a church that's already been sold.

"She let the wrong person in," I said. "Story of this town."

Outside, the el train screamed past on rusted tracks, carrying the last shift home — the night workers, the janitors, the people who clean up other people's messes for a wage that wouldn't cover the dry cleaning on what she was wearing when somebody decided to turn her into a crime scene.

The city doesn't sleep. It just closes its eyes and pretends it can't see what's happening to it.

I pulled my coat collar up and went down the stairs, each step groaning like the whole building was complaining about the inconvenience of still standing. The hallway light buzzed and flickered, making a shadow puppet show of my silhouette against the water-stained plaster.

Another dead woman. Another case number. Another story this city would forget by morning, the way it forgets everything — quickly, conveniently, with a shrug and a move on to the next thing.

But I don't forget. That's my sickness.

I walked out into the 3 AM street, where the puddles reflected neon like open wounds reflecting a sunset, and the air tasted of exhaust and something older — something that was rotting long before she was, and would keep rotting long after I filed my report and the file got buried under newer, shinier tragedies.

This city is a body. She was just the part that finally stopped hiding the decay.

# The Seventh Quarry

The rain came sideways in the Reclamation Zone, slicing between the shattered high-rises like wire. Kael pressed himself into the gap where a stairwell had once been, feeling the rough bite of rebar through his jacket. His lungs burned. The tattoo on his wrist — a barcode, black and precise as a sentence — pulsed in time with his heart.

*Runner 7-14. Status: Active. Elapsed: 4 hours, 22 minutes.*

That's what their drones would say. If he could make it to the canal before sundown, he'd be in the Fringe. Unscannable. Free in the only way the Charter allowed — which was to say, barely.

He heard the hounds first.

Not animals. The Charter didn't waste animals. These were the mechanical kind — low, skeletal things that moved on jointed legs and made a sound like someone cracking their knuckles, over and over, fast. They didn't bark. They didn't need to. The sound alone was enough to turn his blood to slush.

Kael bolted.

He dropped three stories through the collapsed floor of what had been, decades ago, a dentist's office. Old chairs still lined the walls like patients waiting for an appointment that would never come. He hit the ground wrong, felt his ankle fold, and kept moving because stopping meant something worse than pain.

The quarry system was elegant in its cruelty. Debtors, dissidents, the merely unlucky — they were tattooed and released into one of seven Zones, each a ruined quadrant of what had been the eastern seaboard. Hunters paid fortunes for licenses. The Charter called it "Reclamation through Recreation." There were billboards in the clean districts showing smiling hunters in branded gear, thumbs up, a runner blurred in the background. *Earn Your Keep. Hunt the Week.*

Four hours and twenty-two minutes was respectable. Most runners in Zone 3 didn't last two.

He made it halfway across the parking structure — a long concrete shelf cantilevered over nothing — before the net came down.

It dropped from a drone he hadn't seen, a weighted mesh that tangled his legs and arms and brought him crashing to the pavement. The impact knocked the air from his chest. He twisted, fought, but the mesh was smart-fiber; it tightened as he struggled, reading his movements and contracting against them.

"Easy now."

The voice came from above. Measured. Almost kind.

The hunter descended from a utility stairwell on the structure's north end. She was tall, dressed in the charcoal-and-orange kit that marked a Tier-1 licensee — the highest rating, the most expensive permits. # The Weight of Earth

The shelling stopped at dusk, leaving behind that terrible silence—the kind that pressed against the eardrums harder than the explosions ever had. Private Thomas Hale crouched in the firing step of the trench near Saint-Mihiel, his fingers numb inside wool gloves that had stopped being dry three days ago. The mud beneath his boots made sounds like a living thing when he shifted his weight. Breathing. Swallowing.

He was nineteen. He had been a carpenter's apprentice from a small town in Ohio. He had once built a hope chest for his mother's birthday and sanded it so fine you could run your hand across the grain and feel nothing but warmth. That seemed like someone else's memory now, preserved behind glass in a museum he could no longer enter.

The order came down the line in whispers passed from man to man like a bucket brigade of desperate secrecy: *Advance party. Four men. Over the top at 2100 hours. Secure the sap trench fifty yards ahead.*

Fifty yards. In the open. Across wire that might or might not have been cut by the afternoon bombardment. Into a German trench that might or might not still be occupied.

Hale was chosen because he was quiet on his feet. That was what Sergeant Boyle said, clapping him on the shoulder with a hand that trembled visibly. Quiet on his feet. As if that were a skill worth anything in a world made entirely of noise.

---

The four of them went over the parapet into a darkness so complete it felt solid. Hale carried his rifle with bayonet fixed, but in his left hand—his dominant hand—he gripped the entrenching tool. The handle was wrapped in fraying cloth tape. The blade was sharpened on both edges, a modification every man in the company had made on the quiet recommendation of veterans who'd been at the Marne. The shovel was shorter than a rifle, easier to manage in the close quarters of a trench, and it didn't jam when the mud got into it.

These were the things you learned. These were the things that replaced everything you'd known before.

They crossed the broken ground in a low crouch, moving by instinct more than sight. The earth was cratered and strewn with debris—wire, wood, things Hale refused to look at too closely. A flare went up somewhere to the left, bathing the landscape in a ghastly white-green light, and they dropped into the mud and lay perfectly still until it died.

When they reached the German sap trench, they went in over the rear edge, dropping down into it one at a time. The walls were narrow, dug in haste, shored with rough timber that was already bowing under the weight of the earth behind it. The smell hit Hale immediately—exhaust, body odor, the sharp chemical bite of chloride of lime, and beneath it all, something sweet and wrong that he had learned to identify without ever naming it.

Sergeant Boyle went first. Then Corporal Davies. Then a man named Pratt from Pennsylvania who had been a schoolteacher and who had taken to writing letters home in a journal he kept in his breast pocket, letters he would never send because he could not bring himself to describe where he was.

Hale went last.

They moved through the trench in single file, rounding a traverse—a sharp zig in the trench line designed to prevent blast and enfilade fire from traveling down its length—and that was when the world collapsed into a space of six feet and two men.

---

The German came around the corner from the opposite direction. He was alone, as far as Hale could tell, and the two of them met with the sudden intimacy of dancers, close enough to smell each other's breath. The man was small—shorter than Hale, thin, with a face that was mostly eyes in the darkness. He wore a field cap pulled low. He couldn't have been older than seventeen.

What happened next took perhaps four seconds. It felt like four hours.

The German raised his rifle, but the trench was too narrow to bring it to bear properly, and Hale was already inside the arc of the barrel. Hale dropped his own rifle—it was useless at this range, in this space—and swung the shovel.

The first blow caught the German across the forearm as he raised it to protect his head. Hale felt the impact travel up through the handle and into his wrist and shoulder, a jarring vibration like striking a fence post buried in hard clay. The blade bit into flesh and the German made a sound—not a scream, not a shout, but a short, sharp exhalation, the sound of air being forced from lungs by surprise and pain. His rifle clattered into the mud at their feet.

The German grabbed Hale's collar with his good hand and pulled. They staggered together against the trench wall, the timber groaning behind them, and for a moment they were locked together like lovers, close enough that Hale could see the boy's eyes—wide, wet, reflecting what little light existed in that hole in the earth. They were brown. They were terrified. They were exactly like his own.

Hale brought the shovel up between them and drove it into the German's side, just below the ribs. He felt the resistance of the wool uniform, then the momentary resistance of skin, then a yielding—a giving way that was nothing like wood or earth or anything he had ever struck before. The blade went in and the German's body seized, every muscle contracting at once, and his mouth opened in a shape that might have been a word in a language Hale didn't speak.

The boy's fingers clawed at Hale's face, his neck, scrabbling for purchase, for survival, for anything. His nails left burning lines across Hale's cheek. Hale twisted the shovel—he didn't know why, some instinct from some dark ancestral place behind the thinking mind—and the German made a sound like a door hinge that needed oil, a low creaking moan that came from somewhere deeper than the throat.

Then the boy's legs gave out and he slid down the trench wall, and Hale went with him because the shovel was still in him and his hand was still on the handle. They ended up on the floor of the trench, Hale on his knees, the German on his back, the shovel between them like a bridge, like an umbilical cord, like a sin.

The German was still alive. His eyes were open and they were looking at Hale. His mouth moved. His hand came up, slowly, and touched Hale's wrist—not grabbing, not clawing, but resting there, lightly, the way a child rests a hand on a parent's arm in the dark when they are frightened.

Hale pulled the shovel free. The sound it made was a sound he would hear for the rest of his life—a wet, sucking sound, intimate and obscene. Blood followed the blade in a rush that was warm against Hale's knuckles.

The German's hand fell away. His eyes stayed open but the light in them went out like a candle pinched between wet fingers. His chest rose once more, unevenly, and then settled.

Hale knelt there. He knelt there in the mud and the blood and the dark, holding a shovel that was dripping, and he looked at the boy's face, and he could not move.

---

Sergeant Boyle found him there two minutes later. The trench was clear—there had been only the one sentry, a boy left behind when his unit had pulled back during the shelling, a boy who had been alone in the dark waiting for someone to come.

"Hale," Boyle said. Then, louder: "Hale."

Hale looked up. He could see the sergeant's face but couldn't read it. He tried to speak and discovered that his jaw was clenched so tightly the muscles in his temples were vibrating.

"We need to move," Boyle said. He looked at the dead German, then at Hale, then at the shovel. His expression did something complicated and then settled into a careful blankness. "Can you move?"

Hale nodded. He did not think he could move. But he moved. He stood, and his legs held, and he wiped the shovel on the German's coat—a gesture so automatic and so callous that it arrived from somewhere outside himself, from the part of a person that survives when the rest of them has gone away.

They moved back through the trench and over the top and across the fifty yards of broken earth and back into their own lines, and Hale did all of this, and he did not remember any of it later.

---

What he remembered was the hand.

Not the killing. Not the sound or the smell or the warmth of the blood. What came back to him in the hours that followed, and in the days after, and in the nights for years to come, was the moment the boy's hand had rested on his wrist. That gentle pressure. That final, wordless communication between two people who had been trying to kill each other seconds before—a touch that said *I am here* and *I am afraid* and *you are here* and *we are the same*.

He sat in the trench after they returned, his back against the damp wall, the shovel across his knees. Someone gave him a tin cup of tea and he held it but did not drink. Someone else asked him if he was alright and he said yes, and the word came out normally, in the right tone, with the right inflection, and this terrified him more than anything because it meant that the machinery of appearing human was still functioning even while everything behind it had stopped.

He looked at his hands. The left one—the one that had held the shovel—was clean. He had wiped it. He had wiped it on the boy's coat. The right one had blood on the back where the boy had touched his wrist, four faint lines where the nails had scraped, already scabbing over.

He did not wash it. He did not know why. Later, much later, he would understand that it was because washing it would mean acknowledging that it was real, and as long as the blood was there, visible, tangible, he existed in a space between the act and its meaning, a space where he could still pretend that what had happened had happened to someone else.

But the hand. The hand on his wrist. That was his. That had happened to him. Not the killing—he could abstract the killing, could file it under the war, under necessity, under the brutal arithmetic of survival. But the touch was personal. The touch had passed between them like a current, and it had carried something from the boy into Hale and it had stayed there, lodged somewhere behind his sternum, a splinter that would never work its way out.

He was nineteen. He had built a hope chest for his mother. He had sanded it until the grain was smooth as skin.

He sat in the trench and held his cup of tea and did not drink it and did not cry and did not speak, and the war went on around him and inside him and through him, and the boy's face stayed behind his eyes—brown eyes, wide, the cap pulled low, the mouth forming a word he could not hear—and he understood, with a clarity that was almost physical, that he would never again be the person who had built that chest. That person was as dead as the boy in the trench. And the person who remained was someone he did not yet know, someone he would spend the rest of his life discovering, someone who carried a dead boy's touch on his wrist like a brand.

The tea went cold. The shelling started again. Hale did not move.

# The Weight of Bread

## A Scene from the Republic of Solace

The square filled early that morning.

Merchants wheeled their carts into position along the perimeter, selling roasted nuts and candied fruit to the spectators who had already begun staking out the best viewing spots. Children sat on their fathers' shoulders. Off-duty clerks and factory workers pressed toward the front, their faces carrying the particular blankness of routine.

A woman named Petra sold tea from a samovar and did brisk business.

---

The platform had been erected the night before — municipal workers assembling it with the same efficient boredom they brought to repairing cobblestones. The gibbet stood center stage, iron-dark against the pale morning sky. No rope. The Republic preferred the blade. It was faster, the Ministry of Civic Order had declared, and therefore more humane. The word *humane* appeared on a great many official documents these days.

At precisely nine o'clock, the convict was led up the wooden steps.

He was seventeen. His name was Aldo Vass, and he had stolen a loaf of rye bread from a municipal depot eleven days prior. The bread had a stamped value of four credits. The trial had lasted fourteen minutes. His court-appointed defender had spoken for two of those minutes, mostly to confirm his client's identity.

Aldo's wrists were bound before him with plastic restraints. His head had been shaved — a procedural formality, the Ministry explained, to ensure the blade met its mark cleanly. He wore the gray tunic of the unjudged, though judgment had, of course, already been rendered. The tunic was too large for his thin frame, and it billowed slightly in the morning wind.

He looked out at the crowd.

---

The crowd looked back.

What the crowd felt depended entirely on whom you asked, and depending on whom you asked, you would receive a different answer — or no answer at all.

A butcher near the front named Gregor watched with his arms folded, his expression that of a man observing weather. He had seen six of these executions in the past year. The first had sickened him for a week. The second for three days. By the fourth, he had stopped eating breakfast beforehand as a practical matter, but the sickness had passed. Now he simply watched, and if you asked him afterward, he would say something like: *"The law is the law. What can you do?"* He would say this in a tone that dared you to offer an alternative, while quietly hoping you would not.

A young mother, Lida, stood near the back with her hand over her daughter's eyes. The girl was six and kept pulling at her mother's fingers, trying to see. Lida's jaw was set in a way that was either resolve or something she was trying very hard not to name. She would not discuss the execution later. If her husband asked about it that evening, she would say the girl had needed to be shielded, and leave it at that. She would not mention that she had attended voluntarily — that she believed, or wanted to believe, that public example was what kept their streets safe. She would not mention that this belief had grown thinner with each passing month, like cloth rubbed between fingers, and that she was no longer certain it could survive the sight of this particular boy's face.

A teacher named Matthias stood at the edge of the fountain, notebook in hand. He was there, he told himself, to document. He had begun keeping a private record of the executions two years ago — dates, names, crimes, observations of crowd behavior. He told himself it was scholarship. He told himself this with less conviction each time. Today his hand trembled as he wrote the boy's age. *Seventeen.* He stared at the word, then underlined it, then felt sick at having underlined it, as though the act of notation had made him a participant in something he could not yet bring himself to name.

Near the executioner — a municipal employee named Daven who collected clocks as a hobby and was considered by his neighbors to be a gentle, quiet man — stood a cluster of Ministry observers in their dark coats. They watched the crowd more than the platform. Their job was to ensure that the ceremony proceeded with appropriate civic solemnity and that no disturbance — no protest, no fainting that might cascade into unrest, no shout from the crowd — disrupted the State's message.

The State's message was simple: *order is preserved.*

---

Aldo was made to stand at the mark. A Ministry clerk read the charges in a clear, practised voice that carried across the square:

*"Aldo Vass, citizen of the Third Tier, resident of Millwright Lane, having been lawfully convicted under Statute 14, Section 9, of the unauthorized appropriation of state-rationed goods — to wit, one (1) loaf of rye bread, stamped value four (4) credits — and said crime being classified under the Civic Purity Act as a Tier-One offense against collective order, the sentence of public execution is hereby carried out—"*

The clerk read for another minute. The legal language was precise and abundant. It did not mention that Aldo's mother had been ill, or that the ration allocation for his household had been reduced after his father's reassignment to a labor detail, or that the bread had been, at the time of its theft, two days from spoilage. These details were not relevant to the law, and the law was, as Gregor the butcher would say, the law.

Aldo was asked if he wished to make a final statement.

He looked at the crowd again. His mouth opened. Closed. He said, very quietly, words that the microphone caught and carried in a thin, reedy echo across the square:

"I'm sorry, Mama."

Then he was made to kneel.

---

What happened next took four seconds. The blade fell. The sound it made was industrial — a thick, mechanical *thunk*, like a gate closing. There was a collective intake of breath from the crowd, the kind of involuntary gasp that even the most hardened spectators could not fully suppress, followed by a silence that settled over the square like something with weight.

The silence lasted perhaps five seconds. Then life resumed.

The Ministry observers made notes on their clipboards. The clerk signed a document. Gregor the butcher unfolded his arms and turned toward Petra's tea cart. Lida lowered her hand from her daughter's eyes — the girl had been struggling — and said, "It's over," in a voice stripped of inflection. Matthias closed his notebook and stood very still for a long moment, looking at nothing in particular.

A man somewhere in the middle of the crowd — a cabinetmaker, no one important — began to applaud. It was uncertain at first, a scattered clapping, then it caught and spread, and soon most of the crowd was clapping in that uneven, obligatory way that crowds clap when they understand that clapping is expected and that not clapping would be noticed. The Ministry observers did not applaud, but they watched the applauders with something like satisfaction.

Petra poured tea.

---

Within an hour, the platform would be dismantled. By afternoon, the square would look as it always did — merchants, pigeons, children chasing each other around the fountain. The stain where the platform had stood would be washed away by municipal workers using water mixed with lime.

That evening, in a small apartment on Millwright Lane, a woman named Vass would sit at a table that had been set for two and then, after a long moment, set for one. She would not cry. Crying, in the Republic of Solace, was a private act, and she was too exhausted for privacy. She would simply sit, and after a while she would stand, and she would put the extra plate away, and she would go to bed.

On the table, untouched, was a loaf of bread.

---

*The Republic of Solace endured for eleven more years. When it finally collapsed — not through revolution but through the slow, quiet erosion of a citizenry that had stopped believing in anything at all, including its own fear — the execution records were seized and published. Matthias's notebooks were among them. They became required reading in the schools of the republic that followed.*

*The entry for Aldo Vass was three lines long. His age was underlined.*

Look at me. All of you, look at me. Not at the floor. Not at the walls of this room. Look at my eyes. 

I see the trembling in your hands. I see the tears spilling down your beautiful faces. And I love you for it. I love you because your fear is proof of your humanity. But my beloved children, we are gathered here tonight because we have outgrown humanity. We have transcended it. 

Listen to the wind outside. Do you hear it? It doesn’t sound like wind anymore, does it? It sounds like a dying breath. The world out there—the world of concrete, and noise, and hatred, and greed—it is suffocating. You feel it, don’t you? That heavy, crushing weight on your chest every morning when you wake up. The feeling that you were never meant for this place. That you are an alien wearing a skin suit, trying to survive on a planet that has turned against itself. 

You feel that way because it is true. This flesh… this is not who we are. It is a cage. A chrysalis. 

For years, I have taught you how to purify your minds. How to shed the toxins of the outside world. How to elevate your vibrations. But the vibrations of this earth have fallen too low. The dark frequency has won. The outside world is a rotting corpse, and they are trying to pull us down into the grave with them. 

But I won’t let them. I love you too much to let them drag you into the dirt. 

They will tell you, when they find us, that this is a tragedy. The ignorant masses, the media, the blinded shepherds of the old world—they will weep and wail and call this death. But we know the truth, don’t we? We know the secret. 

Death is a lie. It is the ultimate illusion. 

What they call the end is merely the shedding of the cocoon. When the butterfly leaves the chrysalis, does it weep for the husk left behind? No! It flies! It soars into the sun! 

We have spent months preparing the nectar. It is mixed. It is ready. It is not poison; it is a key. When it touches your lips, it will not burn. It will feel like a cool, rushing river washing over your soul. In a matter of moments, the heavy, aching bones will fall away. The pain of the past, the betrayals, the loneliness—all of it will evaporate like morning mist. 

And then, my beautiful lights, you will ascend. 

I have seen it. In my visions, I have stood at the gate of the Tenth Plane. I have felt the warmth of the Source. There is no pain there. There is no hunger, no sickness, no fear. There is only a blinding, perfect, unconditional love. It is a frequency of pure light, and it is waiting for us. It has been waiting for us for centuries. 

But the door is closing. The alignment is tonight. If we do not step through now, we will be trapped here when the final shadow falls. We will be forced to endure the collapse. I cannot let that happen to you. You have given me your trust, and I am honoring that trust by leading you to the promised land. 

Do not look at the cups with fear. Look at them as the vessels of your liberation. 

I will not ask you to do anything I am not willing to do. We will drink together. I will hold your hands as the transition begins. I will be the first to greet you on the other side. I will be standing in the light, waiting to embrace you, to welcome you home. 

So, my children, take your cups. Do not hesitate. Let the old world fall away. Let the shadows stay behind to consume themselves. 

It is time to fly. Drink, and follow me into the eternal.

The smell hit him before he even reached the end of the hallway. It wasn't just a bad odor; it was a physical presence, a thick, humid wall of vapor that seemed to press against his face. It was a suffocating cocktail of sickeningly sweet decay—like overripe melon left to rot in a sealed dumpster—underpinned by the sharp, acrid tang of sulfur, old copper, and raw sewage. The scent of cadaverine and putrescine was so dense he could practically taste it, a greasy film coating the back of his throat and clinging to his tonsils. He pulled the collar of his shirt over his nose, but it did nothing to filter the stench. It infiltrated his pores, heavy and inescapable.

He pushed the bathroom door open. The fluorescent light flickered, illuminating a scene of profound grotesquerie. 

The water in the porcelain tub was no longer water. Seven days of submersion had transformed it into a cloudy, grayish-brown soup, the surface obscured by a thick, iridescent film of human grease and decomposing tissue. A dark, scum-like tide line stained the porcelain just above the waterline.

The body lay submerged beneath the murk, caught in the active throes of decay. In the warm, stagnant water, the bloat had set in with a vengeance. The torso was grotesquely distended, the abdomen swollen tight like a waterlogged drum, filled with the gases of bacterial fermentation. The skin had taken on a ghastly, mottled hue—a sickly patchwork of greenish-black and purplish-red. Dark, branching veins mapped the chest and neck in a process called marbling, standing out starkly against the discolored flesh.

Because it had been submerged, the skin had undergone severe maceration. The epidermis had separated from the layers beneath, blistering and peeling away. The hands and feet were the worst—the skin had ballooned, turning a ghastly, doughy white, wrinkled like laundry left to soak for far too long. It was a phenomenon known as "washerwoman's skin," and on the right hand, the outer layer of flesh had begun to slough off completely, slipping away like a wet, translucent glove to reveal the darker, glossy tissue underneath. The fingernails had detached, resting at the bottom of the tub like tiny discarded shells.

The face was unrecognizable. The features had swollen to twice their normal size, the natural contours smoothed out into a bloated, rubbery mask. The jaw hung slack, pulled down by gravity and the pressure of expanding gases, revealing a swollen, dark-purple tongue that protruded past the lips. A murky, dark fluid leaked from the mouth, mixing with the bathwater. The eyes were half-open, but the corneas had clouded over into a milky, opaque gray, giving the corpse a blind, hollow stare. 

A large clump of the victim's hair had loosened from the scalp, floating on the surface of the water like dark, stringy algae, moving slightly with an imperceptible draft.

Bubbles broke the surface of the murky water—a final, silent release of gas from the rupturing cavities within. The sweet, rotting stench redoubled. Arthur’s stomach violently revolted. He staggered backward out of the doorway, doubling over as the acidic burn of bile rushed up his throat, but even as he retched into the hallway carpet, he knew the smell of that room would haunt him for the rest of his life.

# The Debt

The warehouse smelled like motor oil and old rain. Sal Moretti rolled his sleeves to the elbows and set the aluminum bat against his shoulder like he was walking to the plate on a Sunday afternoon.

Danny Vasquez was already on the concrete floor, back against a support beam, hands up, palms out — the universal language of men who knew what was coming.

"Please." Danny's voice cracked on the single word. "I just need another week. The money's coming. I swear on my—"

"Nobody swears on anything anymore, Danny. That's the problem." Sal popped the bat off his shoulder and let the barrel end tap the floor with a dull *tok*. "You had three weeks. You had three weeks and you had the money, because I know you did, because Carmine saw you at the track Tuesday night dropping four hundred on a trifecta."

Danny's mouth opened and closed. Nothing came out.

"There it is," Sal said. He nodded to Kowalski, standing behind Danny, who grabbed both arms and pinned them back against the beam.

The first swing came low — right shin. The sound was wrong for what it was, not the clean crack people imagine but a wet, dense *thock*, like a mallet into a side of beef. The bone gave with a sound somewhere beneath the flesh, a muffled report that vibrated up through the bat and into Sal's wrists.

Danny didn't scream right away. There was a half-second of silence, his face frozen in simple confusion, as if his leg had just told him a joke he didn't understand. Then the pain arrived — a white, obliterating thing — and the sound that came out of him wasn't a scream so much as a torn-animal shriek that bounced off the corrugated walls and came back to them distorted.

His leg bent where legs don't bend, the shin bowing inward like a parenthesis. His body bucked against Kowalski's grip, one foot scraping uselessly against the floor while the other flopped sideways at an angle that made the whole picture wrong.

"See, the shin's the humanitarian choice," Sal said, almost conversationally. He turned the bat in his hands. "Knee never heals right. Shin, you get plates, you get screws, you walk again in a year. Maybe with a limp. But you walk."

Danny was making a sound now — a low, continuous moan through clenched teeth, spit and snot running down his chin. His eyes had gone somewhere else, rolling, trying to find a ceiling beam to fix on. His hands opened and closed in Kowalski's grip, fingers clawing at nothing.

"The thing is, Danny—" Sal stepped around to the other leg. Danny saw it and started thrashing, his head whipping side to side, a thin thread of words tumbling out — *please please please no no God please* — the words all running together into a single liturgical drone of panic.

"The thing is, it's not about the money anymore." Sal raised the bat. "It's about the *next* guy who thinks about being late."

The second swing mirrored the first — same low arc, same wet *thock*, same delayed silence before the scream. Danny's body seized rigid, then convulsed, then went limp in a way that suggested the conscious part of him had simply checked out, left the room, gone somewhere the bat couldn't reach.

Sal looked down at him. Two legs bent wrong. A man curled on his side, breathing in short, rabbit-fast bursts, a dark stain spreading across the front of his khakis. The sounds now were small — whimpers, wet gurgling breaths, the tick of aluminum cooling against the warehouse air.

Sal pulled a folded business card from his pocket and tucked it into Danny's shirt pocket, right over the heart, the one part of him that still seemed to be working right.

"That's my number," he said. "When you're back on your feet — *if* you're back on your feet — you call me. We start over. Clean slate. No interest."

He tapped the bat twice against his palm, then handed it to Kowalski.

"Get him to County General. Drop him at the entrance. Don't park."

They left the way they came, through the loading dock, into the gray afternoon light. Behind them, the sound of Danny Vasquez's breathing echoed off the walls — shallow, rattling, alive.
